$comment: Machine-readable index of Open Psychology Interactives.
This file is the single source of truth for what has been published.
When you add a tool, append an entry to the matching module's 'tools'
array. Entry fields follow the metadata standard in CLAUDE.md, so a
tool's own metadata.json and its catalogue entry can be kept identical.
assets/js/main.js renders only entries whose status is exactly
recorded here but does not appear on the site, so a work in progress is
never presented as finished. While a module has no published tools its
page keeps its static 'in preparation' message.
See CONTRIBUTING.md for the field-by-field description.

project.name: Open Psychology Interactives
project.description: Free, accessible, classroom-ready browser-based teaching tools for cognitive psychology, research methods, neuropsychology, social and critical psychology, and personality and individual differences.

modules.summary: Tools for the processes students are asked to take on trust: how attention selects, how memory reconstructs rather than replays, and how perception and judgement are shaped by what the system does with limited capacity.

plannedTopics.title: Selective attention and its costs
plannedTopics.detail: What is missed while attending elsewhere, and why the cost is a property of the task rather than of the person.

plannedTopics.title: Working memory capacity
plannedTopics.detail: Holding, manipulating and losing information, and what the limit does and does not predict.

plannedTopics.title: Reconstructive memory
plannedTopics.detail: How recall is assembled at retrieval, and how confidence and accuracy come apart.

plannedTopics.title: Perception as inference
plannedTopics.detail: Why the same input supports more than one interpretation, and what the system does about it.

plannedTopics.title: Judgement under uncertainty
plannedTopics.detail: Heuristics as a sensible response to limited information rather than as simple error.

tools.title: Posner Spatial Cueing
tools.summary: A spatial-cueing experiment the learner performs on themselves: central fixation, a peripheral cue that brightens one of two boxes, and a target that is sometimes where the cue was. Valid, neutral and invalid trials are summarised separately, so the benefit of a valid cue can be told apart from the cost of an invalid one. A seeded worked example reaches every conclusion without performing the task, and the page states repeatedly that eye position is not measured.
learningObjectives: Describe the spatial-cueing paradigm and the role of valid, neutral and invalid trials.
Separate a benefit of valid cueing from a cost of invalid cueing using a neutral baseline.
Explain why a valid-minus-invalid difference conceals which of the two produced it.
Distinguish covert orienting from overt eye movements, and say what evidence would be needed to tell them apart.
Recognise browser reaction times, anticipation cut-offs and small cell sizes as limits on what a classroom block can show.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trials are timed and summarised in the browser tab only, nothing survives a reset, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: No trial is ever timed out - the target persists until answered, nothing animates and nothing flashes, so there is no flicker for a photosensitive reader to encounter and no motion for a reduced-motion rule to switch off. Six untimed practice trials with explanatory feedback run first, and the key mapping is stated before anything begins. Responses accept the Left and Right arrow keys or two buttons at least 3.5rem tall. The cue is carried by three things at once - a much heavier border, the accent colour, and a caret glyph under the box - so it is legible in greyscale and in forced colours. A complete non-timed route exists and is signposted before the task: the seeded worked example fills the same results panel and reaches every conclusion without performing the experiment, which also serves readers for whom the visual display is not usable. The trial display is aria-hidden during a run because a spoken description of a 400 ms cue would arrive after the trial had ended. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table carrying the same numbers; every control has an accessible name; headings do not skip; focus moves to the results heading when a block ends. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
tools.readmeTopic: Spatial cueing: separating the benefit of a valid cue from the cost of an invalid one
tools.simulationNotes: The learner's own block is real timing from their own responses, but in a browser tab: display refresh, keyboard latency and background load add tens of milliseconds, so the numbers are illustrative rather than psychophysical. Responses under 150 ms are treated as anticipations and responses over 2000 ms as lapses; both are counted, reported and excluded from the means. Only correct trials contribute to condition means. The worked example is generated by RT = 340 + condition offset + Normal(0, 45) + Exponential(mean 35), with offsets of -28 for valid, 0 for neutral and +52 for invalid, and accuracies of .98, .97 and .94; n = 96 (48 valid, 32 neutral, 16 invalid) with fixed seed 20260823, so it is identical on every press. It produces valid 348 ms, neutral 374 ms, invalid 440 ms - a benefit of 26 ms and a cost of 66 ms. Those parameters were chosen to make both halves legible with the cost the larger, as it usually is in the literature. They are not a norm, not a published effect size and not anybody's data. The page cannot measure eye position, so nothing here demonstrates covert orienting rather than an unnoticed eye movement, and it says so in the hero panel, the debrief and the teaching notes.

tools.title: Visual Search Laboratory
tools.summary: Learners search original geometric displays for a bar that is tilted and solid. In the feature condition it is the only tilted item; in the conjunction condition half the distractors are tilted and half are solid, so neither property alone identifies it. Set size, target presence, search slopes and target-absent trials are all reported, alongside an untimed panel for looking at displays and a seeded worked example that reaches every conclusion without performing the task.
learningObjectives: Define feature and conjunction search in terms of how the target is specified relative to the distractors.
Read a search function and state its slope in milliseconds per item.
Explain why target-absent trials usually give a steeper slope than target-present trials.
Distinguish a description of a search function from a mechanistic claim about parallel or serial processing.
Recognise how few trials per cell a classroom block provides, and what that does to a slope estimate.
interactionTypes: untimed display inspection with target reveal
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; displays are generated and trials timed in the browser tab only, nothing survives a reset, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: The two properties that define the stimuli are orientation (upright or tilted) and fill (solid or hollow). Neither is a colour, so the paradigm works unchanged in greyscale, with any colour vision deficiency, and in forced-colours mode - no substitute encoding is needed. No trial is timed out: the display persists until answered, nothing animates and nothing flashes. An untimed inspection panel comes before the experiment, where a display can be examined at leisure and the target revealed on request, described in words as well as ringed. Four untimed practice trials with feedback precede the scored block. Responses accept the J and F keys or two buttons at least 3.5rem tall. A complete non-timed route exists and is signposted before the task: the seeded worked example fills the results panel for both conditions on its own. The scored display is aria-hidden because a spoken description would give the answer away and arrive too late to be a search. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables; the two series differ by line style, marker shape and an inline word. Every control has an accessible name; headings do not skip; focus moves to the results heading when a block ends. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
tools.readmeTopic: Feature and conjunction search: set size, search slopes, and what a slope does not prove
tools.simulationNotes: Displays are generated fresh each time from an 8 by 5 grid with per-item jitter, so nothing sits in a predictable place. Set sizes are 8, 16 and 32, half the trials have no target, and a learner's block is 3 trials per cell (18 trials per condition), which is far too few for a stable slope and is described as such throughout. Responses under 200 ms and over 10000 ms are counted, reported and excluded; only correct trials contribute to reaction-time means; slopes are fitted by ordinary least squares to trial-level data. The worked example uses RT = intercept + slope * setSize + Normal(0, sd) + Exponential(tail), with feature intercept 430 and slopes 1.5 (present) and 2.5 (absent), sd 70 and tail 60; conjunction intercept 470 and slopes 24 and 46, sd 90 and tail 70; accuracies .98/.98 and .94/.96; 14 trials per cell per condition with fixed seed 20260825. It produces feature slopes of 2.7 (present) and 3.9 (absent) ms per item and conjunction slopes of 22.4 and 45.2 ms per item. The roughly two-to-one ratio between absent and present slopes is built into the generator rather than discovered, and the page says so: the example illustrates the pattern, it does not evidence it. No parameter here is a norm, a published estimate or anybody's data. Browser timing carries tens of milliseconds of noise, and display size and item spacing are uncontrolled, both of which change search efficiency.

tools.title: Inattentional Blindness
tools.summary: A demanding counting task on a dense static display that also contains a large object nobody was asked about. The learner commits to the count, submits it, answers a recognition question, and only then sees the same display again with everything labelled. Four deterministic variants let a lecturer repeat the demonstration with a different design rather than re-testing the same people, and a demonstrator route reveals the whole thing without spending a variant.
learningObjectives: Distinguish attention from awareness, and report from experience.
Explain why failing to report an unexpected object is not evidence that it was invisible.
Name the design factors that raise and lower noticing rates.
Explain why a single trial cannot measure anybody's attention.
Recognise that a retrospective recognition question is partly a memory test and partly a prompt.
interactionTypes: performed counting task on a static display
transparent replay with the object marked
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the count and the recognition answer stay in the browser tab, nothing is written to storage, and the record of which variants have been used is a JavaScript variable that disappears on reload.
tools.accessibilityNotes: The display is entirely static: nothing moves, nothing flashes, and there is no flicker of any rate, so the demonstration carries no photosensitivity risk and there is no motion for a reduced-motion rule to reduce. The only timed behaviour is an optional 25-second display limit, presented as a checkbox that can be switched off before a run starts, and the tool says plainly that switching it off makes the run fully self-paced. Shape and fill carry the task; no colour carries meaning anywhere. The live display is aria-hidden because a spoken inventory would answer the question being asked, and the reveal afterwards restates the entire display in words - every shape type and count, the object's grid position, and its size relative to the small shapes. Every control has an accessible name; the count field is a labelled number input; the recognition question is a radio group with a visible legend. Headings do not skip; focus moves to the reveal heading. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
tools.readmeTopic: Inattentional blindness: attention, awareness, and a surprise that works exactly once
tools.simulationNotes: Displays are generated deterministically from a fixed seed per variant (20260901 to 20260904) on a 12 by 7 grid with per-item jitter, so a variant is byte-identical every time it is drawn and a whole room can be given the same one. The unexpected object is placed first, never in the middle columns or the middle row, and the cells it would overlap are then kept empty, so a solid star can never hide a countable shape. The counted type is forced to between 6 and 10 instances, so the range stated on the page is always true. Variant A: 48 items, count solid downward triangles, correct count 9, large outlined star. Variant B: 72 items, same count, correct count 9, medium outlined star. Variant C: 48 items, count outlined squares, correct count 6, large outlined star that now shares its fill with the counted set. Variant D: 30 items, count solid downward triangles, correct count 6, large solid star. NO NOTICING RATES ARE REPORTED ANYWHERE. The tool has no data on how often people miss these objects, and an invented percentage would be worse than none; the variant table therefore reports what each variant changes rather than what it produces. Nothing here measures the user: one trial, one binary answer, no reliability and no norms, and the page says so in the reveal and again in the debrief.

tools.title: Change Blindness
tools.summary: Two versions of an original vector street scene alternate, with or without a blank between them. The learner searches for the one difference, says when they have it, and identifies what changed. The same scene can then be re-run with the blank switched off, which is the comparison the tool is built around: the picture is identical, and only the blank has changed.
learningObjectives: Explain what the blank interval does to the local transient produced by a change.
Predict and check how much easier the same change becomes without a blank.
Describe how change type, position and size affect the search.
Explain why change blindness does not show that people store nothing about a scene.
Recognise that a slow search is time spent looking elsewhere, not time spent blind.
interactionTypes: transparent reveal with the change ringed
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; search times and answers stay in the browser tab, nothing is written to storage, and the record of which scenes have been revealed is a JavaScript variable that disappears on reload.
tools.accessibilityNotes: The alternation is deliberately slow: a full cycle is 1.7 seconds (600 ms per view, 250 ms per blank), so the screen changes about 1.2 times a second - well below the three-per-second threshold associated with photosensitive reactions, and much slower than the standard laboratory paradigm. A Pause button is available throughout, and a manual-stepping mode advances only on a button press or the space bar. Under prefers-reduced-motion the tool starts in manual mode and says so in the live region; the phenomenon depends on the blank rather than the speed, so nothing is lost. No CSS animation or transition is used anywhere. Scene parts are distinguished by fill and outline, and the change is always geometric or a lit/unlit state rather than a hue, so the task works in greyscale and in forced colours. The live scene is aria-hidden because describing it aloud would state the answer; the reveal names the change in words and rings it with a dashed circle. Every control has an accessible name; headings do not skip; focus moves to the results heading. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
tools.readmeTopic: Change blindness: what the blank interval does, and what it does not show
tools.simulationNotes: The scenes are original vector drawings generated deterministically from fixed seeds (20260911 to 20260914): a sky, a sun, three clouds, four buildings with grids of lit and unlit windows, three trees and a fence. Nothing is derived from a photograph or any other source. Four trials vary the change on three declared dimensions - a whole tree removed (presence, centre, large); one window's light flipped (state, right edge, small); a building's height raised by an extra storey (size, left edge, large); a cloud moved 96 units sideways (position, upper centre, medium). Those three properties are declared rather than manipulated factorially: with one scene each they are completely confounded with each other and with the scene, and the trial table says so in those words rather than inviting a comparison the design cannot support. The one comparison the design does support is the same scene with and without the blank. Times are the learner's own, in a browser, at an uncontrolled scene size, with an alternation slower than the published paradigm, so they are not comparable with published figures and measure nothing about the person. Each scene works properly once; the tool marks revealed scenes and keeps that record across a reset.

tools.title: Attentional Blink
tools.summary: A rapid stream of consonants contains a digit and, on most trials, the letter X. The learner predicts how second-target accuracy will depend on the gap between the two, runs four slow practice trials and then a block of 25 scored trials, and reads the resulting lag function. Second-target accuracy is reported both over all trials and conditioned on the first target being correct, so the size of that analytic choice is visible. A seeded, simulated worked example reaches every conclusion on the page without running a stream at all.
learningObjectives: Describe the two-target RSVP design and what the lag manipulation varies.
Read a lag function and locate the trough and the recovery.
Explain why second-target accuracy must be conditioned on first-target accuracy.
State what lag-1 sparing is and why it constrains blocking accounts of the effect.
Name at least two accounts of the blink that the lag function cannot distinguish.
interactionTypes: scored block with results withheld until the end
catch trials as a response-bias check
line chart paired with a data table
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trial responses stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Only a single character changes inside a fixed box - the background, size and position are constant, so there is no large-area luminance change of the kind associated with photosensitive reactions, and no CSS animation or transition is used anywhere. Every trial waits indefinitely for both answers, the block can be stopped between trials, and the worked example reaches every conclusion without running a stream, which is the non-timed route the standard requires. Under prefers-reduced-motion the live region says so on load and points to the worked example. The stream box is aria-hidden while running because a glyph changing every 100 ms cannot be usefully spoken. The lag chart is aria-hidden and paired, inside the same figure, with a six-column table giving trials, first-target accuracy and second-target accuracy both overall and conditioned; the two series differ by line style, marker shape and an inline text label, so no meaning rests on colour. Digit and yes/no response buttons are at least 3.25rem tall. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the stream and both chart series. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; the wide results table scrolls inside its own container.
tools.readmeTopic: Attentional blink: the shape of the cost over time, and the accounts it cannot separate
tools.simulationNotes: The learner's own trials are real responses, not simulated: 18-item streams of consonants (X, I, O and Q excluded from the distractor set), a digit from 2 to 7 at stream position 5, 6 or 7, and the letter X at lag 1, 2, 3, 5 or 8 after it. A block is 25 trials - four per lag plus five catch trials with no X, which is the check on a yes bias. Item duration is 100 ms by default, with 140 ms and 180 ms offered as gentler rates that genuinely shrink the effect. Practice trials run at 220 ms with immediate feedback. Four trials per lag is far too few for a stable estimate; that is deliberate, stated in the results panel, and the reason the worked example exists. The worked example is simulated with mulberry32 seeded at 20260935: 48 trials per lag plus 40 catch trials, first-target accuracy 0.88, second-target detection given a correct first target of 0.86, 0.48, 0.41, 0.72 and 0.88 at lags 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8, detection 0.15 higher when the first target was missed, and a false-alarm rate of 0.08 on catch trials. Lag-1 sparing is therefore built into the generator rather than discovered, and the results panel, the debrief and the challenge all say so. These numbers are illustrative: they are not norms, not published estimates and not anybody's data. Browser timing is a request rather than a guarantee, so item durations are approximate and the tool says so.

tools.title: Stroop Interference Laboratory
tools.summary: An original colour-word interference task. The learner predicts where the neutral condition will sit, runs practice trials and then a scored block naming ink colours, and reads a summary that splits the usual single Stroop effect into interference above the neutral baseline and facilitation below it. A trial-mix setting turns the proportion-congruency manipulation into something the learner can run rather than be told about, and a transfer challenge asks what four further changes to the task would do to the effect.
learningObjectives: Separate interference from facilitation using a neutral baseline.
Explain what a single incongruent-minus-congruent difference score hides.
Predict how the effect changes when the proportion of incongruent trials changes.
Describe the asymmetry between naming the ink and reading the word.
Explain why a Stroop difference score is not a measure of a person's cognitive control.
interactionTypes: scored block with results withheld until the end
trial-mix manipulation the learner can run
bar chart paired with a data table
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; reaction times and answers stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
tools.accessibilityNotes: The task requires discriminating ink colours, which is the phenomenon rather than a design accident and cannot be removed. Three routes are provided instead: a two-colour set (blue and yellow, which differ in brightness as well as hue), a stimulus panel with one fixed near-black background in both the light and dark site palettes so every ink sits at 7:1 contrast or better, and a worked example that reaches every conclusion on the page without responding to a single colour. Away from the stimulus itself nothing depends on colour: every response button prints its colour name in words alongside its swatch, the chart bars print their own values and the incongruent bar is hatched as well as differently filled, and all results are given as numbers in a table. One word is on screen at a time and it stays until the learner answers - no trial is timed out, nothing fades, moves or animates, and no CSS animation or transition is used, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. Responses can be given by pointer or by the number keys printed on the buttons; response targets are 3.25rem tall. The stimulus panel is aria-hidden during a run because any useful description of it would state the answer. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the panel, the swatches and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; the wide results table scrolls inside its own container.
tools.readmeTopic: Stroop interference: what a neutral baseline adds, and what a difference score is not
tools.simulationNotes: The learner's own trials are real responses, not simulated. Stimuli are original: colour words printed in their own colour (congruent), in a different colour from the set (incongruent), or common non-colour nouns printed in one of the inks (neutral). Neutral items are matched to the colour words only approximately in length, and not at all in frequency or orthographic neighbourhood; the teaching notes say so. Inks are rotated rather than sampled within each condition, so ink identity carries no information about condition. A block is 24, 36 or 60 trials, split a third each way in the balanced mix and one sixth, one sixth, two thirds in the mostly-incongruent mix. Correct responses between 200 ms and 3000 ms enter the condition means; errors, anticipations and lapses are counted and reported separately rather than averaged in. The worked example is simulated with mulberry32 and Box-Muller: RT = base + condition offset + Normal(0, 70) + Exponential(mean 60), floored at 260 ms. Block A is a balanced mix, seed 20260923, 80 trials per condition, base 620, offsets -22 / 0 / +78, accuracy .98 / .97 / .93, and produces interference +78 ms and facilitation +24 ms. Block B is a mostly-incongruent mix, seed 20260987, 30 / 30 / 120 trials, base 640, offsets -6 / 0 / +38, accuracy .97 / .97 / .95, and produces interference +35 ms and facilitation +3 ms. Both seeds were chosen so the sample means land near the generator's parameters; the page says so and treats it as a teaching point about sampling rather than hiding it. The smaller effect in Block B is built into the generator to illustrate proportion congruency, not discovered by it. These numbers are illustrative: they are not norms, not published effect sizes and not anybody's data, and browser display and input timing are uncontrolled.

tools.title: Dichotic Listening and Selection Theories
tools.summary: A visual analogue of the competing-message paradigm, with an optional stereo tone layer synthesised in the browser. Two word streams run side by side; the learner monitors one and ignores the other, and one item in the ignored stream is planted. Two questions after each trial keep apart a physical judgement (did anything look different?) and identification of meaning (which word was it?). The attended-task rule is the load manipulation, and a seeded simulated class dataset supplies the pattern that one person's four trials cannot.
learningObjectives: Distinguish detection of a physical change in an ignored channel from identification of its meaning.
Describe what happens to both when the attended task is made harder.
Explain which findings early selection, attenuation and late selection were each built to handle.
Explain why failure to report is weak evidence for absence of processing.
Recognise why a theory that absorbs every finding is not thereby supported by them.
interactionTypes: run with results withheld until the end
optional synthesised stereo audio with a full transcript
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trial responses stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage. The optional tones are generated by oscillators in the page and involve no audio files and no network request.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Items change once every 800 ms - about 1.25 changes a second, well below the three-per-second threshold associated with photosensitive reactions - and only the two words change; the panels, their size and their position stay put. No CSS animation or transition is used anywhere, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. The attended side is marked three ways at once: a heavier border, a filled label reading Attend to this, and a caret glyph in that label, none of which is a hue. The physically marked item is larger, bolder and underlined, again not a hue. Audio is off by default, opt-in, synthesised from oscillators with low gains, and preceded by a Test the sound button which also switches the trial tones on so that a successful headphone check cannot be followed by a silent task; every trial is followed by a full transcript of both streams, which is the text alternative for both the visual stream and the tones. The live stream area is aria-hidden while running because reading both sides aloud would defeat the selection the task is about. Responses are by pointer or the space bar, with targets at least 3.25rem tall, and no trial is timed out at the response end. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a five-column table; its two series differ by fill, by a hatch and by the printed value. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the stream panels and both chart series. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
tools.readmeTopic: Selective attention: what gets through from an ignored channel, and which theory each finding troubles
tools.simulationNotes: The learner's own trials are real responses, not simulated. A trial is 16 item pairs at 800 ms; the probe sits at pair 9, 10 or 11 and varies on two factors, marked or plain and relevant (an animal, the monitored category) or unrelated. A run is four trials, one per probe type. The attended-task rule is the load manipulation: press for every animal, or press for every animal except birds. The attended item at the probe position is always a non-target, so attended load at that moment is constant across trials. Recognition offers the probe plus five foils drawn from pools disjoint from both streams, always two animals and four non-animals so the option set never gives the answer away. Only the learner's first trial is naive; the tool reports it separately and says why. The worked example is a simulated class of 40 fictional participants with one trial per cell, mulberry32 seed 20260955, drawn as Bernoulli trials: looked different .88 and .72 for marked items under one and two rules, .17 and .10 for plain items; word recognised .62/.38, .55/.30, .34/.14 and .13/.06 for marked-relevant, marked-unrelated, plain-relevant and plain-unrelated. The two questions are drawn independently in the generator, which is a deliberate simplification - in real data they would be correlated, and the simulated plain-relevant cell accordingly shows recognition above noticing. That pattern is built in to illustrate the shape of the classic findings; it is not evidence for them, not a norm, and not anybody's data. The whole task is a visual analogue: written columns are not two spoken messages at two ears, and the tones carry separation but no words.

tools.title: Dual-Task and Limited Capacity Laboratory
tools.summary: Two simple choice tasks - a letter judged vowel or consonant, a number judged odd or even - performed alone and then together. The three blocks run in a fixed order so that every dual-task cost is measured against the learner's own single-task baseline. Two settings turn the laboratory into an argument: making the number task harder without changing its response, and removing its per-item choice response altogether. The results panel reports the cost to each task separately, so an asymmetric cost is visible rather than averaged away.
learningObjectives: Measure a dual-task cost against its own single-task baseline.
Read an asymmetric cost and say what question it raises.
Predict what happens when the second task no longer needs a choice response.
Distinguish a general-capacity account from a structural bottleneck by their predictions.
Explain why multitasking ability cannot be inferred from one short run.
interactionTypes: enforced block order with a stage track
counting version with a single end-of-block report
results withheld until each block ends
bar chart paired with a data table
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; response times and answers stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
tools.accessibilityNotes: No display is ever timed out - each waits for its response - and nothing on the page animates or transitions, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. Only the two glyphs change; the panel, its size and its position stay put. The number sits directly above the letter and both are centred, so neither task needs an eye movement to reach the other. Responses are by pointer or by the keys printed on the buttons (F and J for the letter, D and K for the number, space for the counting version), each button carries an explicit accessible name, and the key hint itself is aria-hidden decoration. Response targets are 3.25rem tall. Nothing depends on colour: the stage track marks the current block with a border, a background and aria-current=step as well as a number; chart bars print their own values and the combined bars are hatched as well as differently filled; all results are numbers in a table. The trial display is aria-hidden during a block because a live description would state the answer. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a six-column table. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the display, the answered-state marker and both chart series. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; the wide results table scrolls inside its own container.
tools.readmeTopic: Dual-task costs: baselines, asymmetry, and why multitasking is not a trait
tools.simulationNotes: The learner's own blocks are real responses, not simulated. A block is 20 trials; the inter-trial interval is 500 ms and no display is timed out. Letters are drawn 50/50 from vowels and consonants; numbers are a single digit 1-9 in the easy setting and a two-digit number 12-98 judged on the parity of its digit sum in the hard setting, which adds processing without changing the response set. In the counting version there is no per-item choice response: block 2 is paced by a single non-choice Next press, which gives a viewing time per number, and in block 3 the number is on screen for exactly as long as the letter response takes, so no separate number time is reported there and the informative number measure is the count itself. Correct responses between 200 ms and 4000 ms enter the means; errors, anticipations and lapses are counted and reported separately. Block 3 always follows blocks 1 and 2, so the cost is measured against baselines collected when the learner was less practised - a confound the design cannot remove, stated in those words in the limits panel. The worked example is one simulated participant who ran both settings, with RT = base + Normal(0, 80) + Exponential(mean 55) floored at 220 ms. Set A (respond mode, easy, seed 20260971, 60 trials per block) uses bases 610/780 for letters and 570/850 for numbers with accuracies .97/.93 and .96/.90, and produces a cost of +130 ms to letters and +273 ms to numbers. Set B (counting mode, easy, seed 20260972) uses bases 610/690 for letters and 700 for the number viewing time, with counting errors of 0 alone and 2 in the dual block, and produces a letter cost of +98 ms. The asymmetry in Set A and the much smaller letter cost in Set B are built in to illustrate the shape of the classic findings; they are not evidence for them, not norms and not anybody's data. Browser display and input timing are uncontrolled.

tools.title: Working-Memory Load Laboratory
tools.summary: The learner holds two, four or six items across a fixed retention interval, makes three quick judgements while holding them, and then answers one recognition probe. Material (letters or grid positions) crosses with concurrent task (syllable judgement, symmetry judgement or nothing), so a same-domain pair can be compared with a different-domain pair of identical pacing. The tool reports a load function for each run and accumulates runs in a comparison table, and it says throughout that it operationalises a demand rather than measuring anybody's capacity.
learningObjectives: Read a load function and describe it as a curve rather than a fixed number of slots.
Explain why a same-domain concurrent task costs more than a different-domain one of equal pacing.
Distinguish storage load, attentional control and task similarity as explanations.
Identify findings that a design of this kind cannot speak to.
Explain the difference between operationalising a demand and measuring a capacity.
interactionTypes: paced concurrent judgements in a fixed retention interval
seeded simulated class dataset covering all four combinations
line chart paired with a data table
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; responses stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
tools.accessibilityNotes: The display changes at most once every 1.8 seconds and only its contents change; the panel, its size and its position stay put. Nothing fades, moves or animates and no CSS animation or transition is used anywhere, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. Only the concurrent judgements are paced, and they are paced deliberately so that the retention interval is the same length in every condition, including the do-nothing baseline; the recognition probe is never timed out and the worked example reaches every conclusion without running a trial. Nothing depends on colour: filled grid cells differ from empty ones in fill and the probed cell is marked by a thick dashed ring as well, the symmetry pattern is drawn in the text colour with a dashed mirror line, and chart points are squares carrying their own printed percentage. The trial display is aria-hidden because reading it aloud would be the answer. Response buttons are rebuilt for each phase with their answer written in words and are at least 3.25rem tall. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a five-column table. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading and to the first response button of each phase, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the display, the grid, the pattern and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
tools.readmeTopic: Working-memory load: storage, control and similarity are three different things
tools.simulationNotes: The learner's own trials are real responses, not simulated. A trial is 2500 ms of encoding, a retention interval of three judgements at a fixed 1800 ms each (or an equal blank wait in the do-nothing condition), and one untimed recognition probe with a 50 per cent chance of being in the set. Holding decay time constant across conditions is the reason the judgements are paced. Loads are 2, 4 and 6 items with four trials each; material is a set of consonants or a set of cells in a 4x4 grid; the concurrent task is a two-syllable judgement on a printed word (verbal) or a left-right symmetry judgement on a pattern (visuospatial). Symmetric patterns are built by mirroring two columns and asymmetric ones by flipping exactly one cell, so the two kinds have the same density on average. Missed judgements are recorded as misses rather than dropped. The worked example is four simulated classes of 100 fictional participants contributing four trials per load each, so 400 observations per cell, with mulberry32 seeds 20260991 to 20260994. Memory accuracy by load is set at 0.95 / 0.80 / 0.66 for letters with syllables, 0.96 / 0.90 / 0.82 for letters with symmetry, 0.94 / 0.79 / 0.64 for positions with symmetry and 0.96 / 0.89 / 0.81 for positions with syllables; concurrent-task accuracy is 0.86 in the same-domain runs and 0.93 in the different-domain runs, and concurrent-task time is 1080 ms or 940 ms plus 30 ms per item held. The values at two items are deliberately equal across runs because there is little to interfere with at that load, and the selective-interference gap opens at four and six. That pattern is built into the generator to illustrate the classic finding; it is not evidence for it, not a norm and not anybody's data. The tool operationalises a demand and says so; it does not estimate working-memory capacity, and it does not manipulate attentional control at all.

tools.title: False Memory and Source Monitoring
tools.summary: The learner studies three original themed lists of eight items, each item labelled with one of two named sources, and is then tested on twelve words: six studied, three related words that were never presented, and three unrelated words that were never presented. Recognition, confidence and source attribution are collected as three separate judgements and reported as three separate measures, because the places where they come apart are the finding. A transfer challenge asks what changing source distinctiveness, delay, forewarning and list length would do to each measure.
learningObjectives: Separate recognition, confidence and source attribution as three measures that can diverge.
Explain a gist-based intrusion without claiming that memory is unreliable.
Describe source monitoring as an inference made at retrieval rather than a stored label.
Use an unrelated-new baseline to interpret an endorsement rate.
Predict how source distinctiveness, delay, warning and list length affect each measure differently.
interactionTypes: recognition and confidence in a single judgement
unrelated-new baseline as a bias check
bar chart paired with a data table
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; study and test responses stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage. The record of which themes have been used is a JavaScript variable that survives a reset within the tab and disappears on reload.
tools.accessibilityNotes: The study card changes once every 1.5 to 3 seconds at the learner's chosen pace and only its contents change; the card, its size and its position stay put. The test phase is not timed at all, and no CSS animation or transition is used anywhere, so there is nothing for a reduced-motion setting to switch off. The two sources are distinguished by their full name printed above every studied word and by a solid or dashed left rule - never by hue. Response buttons state their answer in words including the confidence level, carry an explicit accessible name naming the word being judged, and are at least 3rem tall. The stage track marks the current phase with a border, a background and aria-current=step as well as a number. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a five-column table; each bar prints its own percentage and mean confidence, and the related-word bar is hatched as well as differently filled. The study card is aria-hidden while presenting. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading and to the first option of each question, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the card, the test word and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
tools.readmeTopic: False memory and source monitoring: recognition, confidence and source can disagree
tools.simulationNotes: All word lists are original to this tool: six themes of eight items each, with a critical lure per theme that is never presented. No published word list is reproduced. A run uses three themes not yet spent, so the demonstration can be run fresh exactly twice; the tool tracks and reports how many fresh themes remain, and that record deliberately survives a reset because a theme a learner has already studied is no longer fresh material. Within each theme, four items come from each source, so source is not confounded with theme, and themes are presented blocked. The test set is six studied items (two per theme), three critical lures and three unrelated words, shuffled. Recognition and confidence are collected in a single click (not seen / seen and guessing / seen and fairly sure / seen and certain) and source is asked only of endorsed items, with an explicit I-cannot-tell option. The unrelated-new row is the response-bias check and the limits panel says that the raw rates are not corrected for bias. The worked example is a simulated class of 60 fictional participants with mulberry32 seed 20261001: endorsement .84 for studied items, .61 for lures and .09 for unrelated items; confidence given endorsement distributed with certain at .62 / .38 / .08 and fairly-sure thresholds at .92 / .80 / .35; source correct on .71 of placed studied items; and 72 per cent of endorsed lures and unrelated items given a source they never had. It produces 85 per cent, 61 per cent and 11 per cent endorsement with mean confidences of 2.5, 2.2 and 1.4 out of 3, and 70 per cent source accuracy on studied items. That pattern is built in to illustrate the classic finding; it is not evidence for it, not a norm and not anybody's data. The tool deliberately avoids framing any of this as evidence that memory is unreliable.

tools.title: Decision Framing Laboratory
tools.summary: Four fictional decisions about stock at risk - seedlings, servers, grain and hire bicycles - each offering a safe option and a gamble with identical expected outcomes. Two are written as gains and two as losses, assigned at random, and the equivalence is withheld until all four decisions are made. The learner can set how certain the safe option is and how the stock is described, and the reveal prints each decision beside the wording that was not shown. A seeded simulated class supplies the aggregate pattern that four decisions cannot, and the challenge asks the learner to rewrite a scenario so the framing matters less.
learningObjectives: State what a framing effect is in terms of a reference point.
Explain why the certainty of the safe option matters independently of its safety.
Distinguish a robust aggregate shift from a claim about any individual.
Rewrite a decision problem so that the framing asymmetry is smaller.
Say why a framing effect is not by itself evidence of irrationality.
interactionTypes: side-by-side reframing of each decision made
bar chart paired with a data table
constructive rewriting challenge with live output
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; decisions stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, and nothing is written to storage.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing in this tool is timed and nothing moves; there is no CSS animation or transition anywhere, so a reduced-motion preference has nothing to switch off. The two options are large text blocks rather than small controls, because each carries a sentence that has to be read before choosing; each is labelled Option A or Option B in words as well as carrying its own description. Nothing depends on colour: the chart bars print their own percentages and the loss-framed bars are hatched as well as differently filled, and the reveal sets the two framings side by side as text. The chart is aria-hidden and paired inside the same figure with a four-column table. The challenge uses native checkboxes with visible labels and per-item text feedback, and the rewritten scenario it produces is rendered as ordinary readable text. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, focus moves to the results heading and to the first option of each scenario, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the scenario card, the reframe panels and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; wide tables scroll inside their own containers.
tools.readmeTopic: Framing and reference dependence: identical arithmetic, two descriptions, different choices
tools.simulationNotes: The four scenarios are fictional and deliberately contain no people, so that nothing turns on how a reader feels about the stakes - which is also why the limits panel says nothing here generalises to decisions where the stakes are the point. Every stock is divisible by 27 (810, 540, 1080 and 1620) so that all quantities are whole numbers: the safe option saves exactly a third of the stock, the very-likely version offers a 90 per cent chance of saving a third divided by 0.9, and the gamble offers a 1 in 3 chance of saving everything. All three have the same expected outcome. Frames are assigned at random, two gains and two losses, so each scenario is seen once and no within-person comparison is possible; the reveal therefore prints the unseen framing beside each decision. The reference-point setting changes no number and is deliberately not modelled in the worked example, because inventing a small effect would be worse than reporting none; the results prose says so and turns it into a question about which reference point the learner actually used. The worked example is simulated with mulberry32 seed 20261011: 300 fictional participants in each certainty condition making four decisions each, so 600 decisions per cell, with the safe option chosen at rates of 0.74 and 0.52 in the gain frame and 0.33 and 0.27 in the loss frame for the certain and very-likely versions. It produces 74, 53, 33 and 29 per cent. Both the framing effect and the certainty effect are built in to illustrate two well-replicated findings; they are not evidence for them, not norms and not anybody's data, and the debrief is explicit that replication size varies with wording, sample and domain.

tools.title: Human Attention versus AI Attention
tools.summary: Three stages on one sentence. The learner first resolves an ambiguous pronoun in two sentences that differ in three words, and notices that the resolution was fast and reportable. They then compute scaled dot-product attention weights over the same sentence by choosing a position, a head, a softmax temperature and whether later positions are masked. A sorting challenge over eight statements closes the loop: two are true of both, two of neither, and those four mark exactly where the analogy holds and where it fails.
learningObjectives: State precisely what a transformer attention weight is, in arithmetic terms.
Name two respects in which the two uses of the word genuinely correspond.
Name four respects in which they do not, including awareness and the cost of division.
Explain why a map of attention weights is not an explanation of a model's output.
Recognise when a shared technical word is doing argumentative work it has not earned.
interactionTypes: bar chart paired with a text equivalent and a full data table
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; answers and settings stay in the browser tab as JavaScript variables and disappear on reload, nothing is written to storage, and no model or external service is contacted at any point.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing in this tool is timed and nothing moves; there is no CSS animation or transition anywhere, so a reduced-motion preference has nothing to switch off. Nothing depends on colour: the query position in the token strip is marked by a heavier border, a filled background and the word query printed under it; masked positions are marked by a dashed border and the word masked; chart bars print their own percentage and the query row carries a dashed outline as well as a different fill. The chart is aria-hidden and paired, inside the same figure, with an always-visible paragraph stating the three largest weights, the smallest, the number of masked positions and the fact that the weights sum to 100 per cent, plus the full five-column table one click away in a details element. The temperature range carries an aria-valuetext in words. The interactive uses a pinned primary block so the token strip and the chart stay in view while the controls column is scrolled. Stage 1 and stage 2 are revealed progressively and focus moves to each new heading as it appears. Every control has an accessible name, headings do not skip, and forced-colours rules are supplied for the token strip and the chart. Usable at 320px and at projector widths with no horizontal page scroll; the wide table scrolls inside its own container.
tools.readmeTopic: Human attention and transformer attention: one word, two different things
tools.simulationNotes: No model is run and nothing is learned. The sentence - the cyclist passed the lorry because it was moving slowly - is cut into ten tokens, each given a hand-written key vector of three numbers, and three heads are defined as three multipliers each. The computation is genuine scaled dot-product attention as implemented: the query vector is the query token's key vector multiplied elementwise by the head, each score is the dot product with a token's key vector divided by the square root of three, masked positions are set to minus infinity, and the weights are a softmax of the scores divided by the temperature. There are no value vectors, no residual stream, no feed-forward layers and no second layer, and the limits panel says so. Every number was chosen by the author so that the three presets produce three legible pictures, and the page states this in the hero badge, the interactive brief, a dedicated provenance panel and the limits panel: the apparent meaningfulness of the first preset is manufactured, and in a real model these values are learned, nobody chooses what a coordinate means, and many heads produce patterns that resist description. The three coordinates are deliberately never given names, because naming a learned coordinate after the thing it appears to track is the interpretive error the tool exists to make visible. Reference values, verified against the running tool: at position 7 with head A and temperature 1.00 the weights are lorry 35.4 per cent, cyclist 18.5 per cent and it 12.9 per cent; the first preset (head A, temperature 0.60) gives lorry 56.4 per cent; the second (head B, temperature 0.60, masked) gives it 23.1 per cent, because 18.1 per cent and lorry 17.8 per cent with three positions masked; the third (head C, temperature 2.50) gives every position between 9 and 11 per cent.

modules.summary: Tools for design and inference: how much a statistic moves from sample to sample, what uncertainty around an estimate means, and what a test statistic is actually responding to.

plannedTopics.title: Sampling distributions
plannedTopics.detail: Repeatedly drawing samples from a known population and watching the distribution of the sample mean take shape.

plannedTopics.title: Confidence intervals
plannedTopics.detail: What the interval covers across repeated samples, and what it does not say about a single study.

plannedTopics.title: p-values and significance testing
plannedTopics.detail: How a p-value responds to effect size, sample size and variability, held apart one at a time.

plannedTopics.title: Correlation and regression
plannedTopics.detail: Building a scatterplot point by point to see how outliers, range restriction and non-linearity move the coefficient.

plannedTopics.title: Statistical power
plannedTopics.detail: The trade-off between sample size, effect size and the chance of detecting a real effect.

tools.title: Research Question to Method Mapper
tools.summary: Six fictional research questions, read one at a time. For each, the learner decides what kind of claim the question is trying to support, whether it is qualitative, quantitative or mixed, what design it implies, and what they would still need to know before naming an analysis. Feedback addresses each part separately and marks readings as well supported, defensible or hard to defend rather than right or wrong. No statistical test is ever named.
learningObjectives: Identify what kind of claim a research question is trying to support before considering any analysis.
Distinguish description, difference, association, prediction, explanation and interpretation as research aims.
Explain why the same data structure can require different treatment depending on the design that produced it.
Name the further information a method choice depends on, including nesting, allocation, measurement and epistemological position.
Recognise a genuinely ambiguous research question and say what would settle it.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native selects, radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. The research question and a running summary of the learner's reading are pinned to the top of the stage so both stay visible while the four controls are set. Feedback states its standing in words - 'Well supported', 'Defensible', 'Hard to defend from this wording' - so the coloured left border is a redundant cue. Progress through the six questions is shown in a stage track where the current and completed steps are named in visually hidden text as well as marked. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; focus moves to newly revealed headings; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths; forced-colours rules provided.
tools.readmeTopic: Reading a research question: what claim it makes, what design could support it, and what you still need to know
tools.simulationNotes: Six invented research questions with invented settings and sample sizes. There is no score and no single answer key: each option for each question carries a standing of well supported, defensible or hard to defend, with a written note explaining what that reading would commit the researcher to. Part four - what you still need to know - uses a different set of standings: decisive, reasonable, already answered in the description, or not bearing on this question. Question six is deliberately ambiguous, with explanation and interpretation both marked well supported and all three of qualitative, quantitative and mixed defensible, because the wording does not contain the commitment that would settle it. No statistical test is named anywhere in the tool. No real study, dataset, department or researcher is described.

tools.title: Operationalisation Laboratory
tools.summary: Three fictional constructs, each modelled as five facets, and six candidate operational definitions apiece drawn from self-report, behavioural-trace, observational and performance-based families. Ticking measures moves a live facet coverage map and a plain-language list of what each measure also records. Coverage rises as measures are added, and so does reactivity, while feasibility falls - and full coverage of a facet list is still not the construct.
learningObjectives: Explain why an operational definition is a claim about a construct rather than a translation of it.
Distinguish construct under-representation from construct-irrelevant variance and give an example of each.
Describe the reactivity and feasibility costs of getting closer to a construct.
Say what combining measures from different families buys, and what it does not.
Identify a design in which the intervention acts directly on the outcome measure.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native select, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. The facet coverage map is built from HTML rather than an image: each row prints its facet name and its standing in words - not reached, partly reached, well reached - so the bar length and the fill colour are both redundant cues. Numeric summaries appear in a definition list beside the map. The map and readout are pinned to the top of the stage so they stay visible while the measure list is worked through. Every change is announced through the shell's polite live region with a full sentence, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, reduced motion is honoured for the bar transition, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Operationalisation: what a measure reaches, what it misses, and what it quietly records instead
tools.simulationNotes: Three constructs - academic engagement, stress and social connection - each modelled as five named facets, with six candidate measures apiece. Each measure carries a coverage level per facet of 0, 1 or 2, plus a reactivity and a feasibility rating on a three-point scale and a written list of what else it records. For a selected plan the facet level is the maximum across the selected measures rather than the sum, because two partial measures of one facet do not add up to a good one. Plan reactivity is the highest among the selected measures and plan feasibility the lowest, reduced one step further for each measure beyond two. The coverage percentage is arithmetic on the facet list shown above it: it is not a validity coefficient and the page says so. The facet lists are teaching simplifications and are contested for all three constructs. No published instrument, item or proprietary assessment is reproduced; measures are described generically.

tools.title: Confound Detective
tools.summary: Three fictional studies with confident causal claims, each run in two phases. First the learner classifies five variables as confounds, nuisance variables, part of the manipulation or held constant, and receives a written note on each. Then a repair bench opens: ticking design fixes redraws a causal diagram and moves the estimated effect back towards a true effect only the tool knows. One repair in every study - recruiting more participants - is there to be seen doing nothing at all.
learningObjectives: State the two conditions a variable must meet before it can bias a comparison.
Distinguish a confound from a nuisance variable, from part of the manipulation and from a constant.
Explain why increasing sample size fixes noise and cannot fix bias.
Compare what randomisation and statistical adjustment each require in order to work.
Choose a design repair that removes a named bias rather than one that only improves precision.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native selects, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. The causal diagram is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving every confound, its status in words - open, partly blocked with a percentage, or blocked - and the bias it is contributing; blocked nodes in the diagram carry a dashed outline and the word 'blocked' inside the node as well as a muted stroke. The two effect bars print their own name and their own number, and are distinguished by a stripe pattern as well as by fill. The study card and, once the repair bench opens, the estimate are pinned to the top of the stage so both stay visible while the controls below are worked through. Every repair announces a full sentence including the new estimate through the polite live region. Reduced motion is honoured for the bar transitions, forced-colours rules are provided for every diagram and bar class, focus moves to the detective heading when it unlocks, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Confounds, nuisance variables and design repair: why more data cannot fix bias
tools.simulationNotes: Three invented studies - a revision app, a hospital ward audit and a typeface experiment - covering between-groups confounding, confounding by indication in observational data, and order and material confounds in a within-participants design. Each study has a true effect known only to the tool plus a fixed bias per confound; the estimate is the true effect plus the sum of the unblocked biases. A repair removes a stated fraction of a named confound's bias, and fractions from several repairs combine multiplicatively rather than adding. Precision is tracked separately as a multiplier on interval width, so noise and bias move independently on screen. One repair in every study blocks nothing and only improves precision. The bias figures are invented to make the argument legible and are not estimates of confounding in any real study; real confounds interact and sometimes cancel, and keeping them additive here is a deliberate simplification. No real module, ward, trial, patient or dataset is described.

tools.title: Sampling Bias Simulator
tools.summary: A generated population of 4,000 fictional students whose true average weekly study hours is printed on screen. Learners recruit from it by convenience, self-selection, year quotas, stratified random sampling or simple random sampling, set how much more likely commuters and students with jobs are to decline, and watch repeated estimates land on a number line beside the truth. Raising the sample size tightens the cloud of estimates without moving it, which is the whole distinction between variability and bias.
learningObjectives: Separate sampling variability from systematic selection bias using repeated draws from a known population.
Explain why increasing the sample size narrows the interval and cannot move a biased estimate.
Describe what a quota corrects and what it leaves untouched.
State the condition a probability sample still needs in order to remain unbiased.
Identify which practical changes to a survey reduce bias rather than scatter.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the population is generated and every sample drawn in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios, ranges, a number input and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; the two sliders announce meaningful values such as '90 per cent tilt: commuters and students with jobs are that much more likely to decline'. The estimate line is hidden from assistive technology and every figure it carries is repeated in a definition list beneath it - population mean, current estimate, difference from truth, and the running average of all draws - plus a full table of every draw behind a disclosure control. On the line itself the truth is a solid rule with its own printed value, previous estimates are hollow circles and the current estimate is a filled diamond with an interval bar, so shape rather than colour carries the distinction. The composition table names each group and prints both population and sample percentages. Every draw announces a full sentence through the polite live region. Focus moves to the simulator heading when it unlocks, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Sampling bias against sampling variability: why a bigger sample cannot fix the wrong people
tools.simulationNotes: A population of 4,000 fictional students generated once from a fixed seed of 20260807, so its true mean of 11.29 weekly study hours is identical in every browser. Each student has a year of study, a commuting status and a part-time job, and hours are 12.6 plus year effects, minus 2.2 for commuting and 3.0 for a job, plus normal noise with a standard deviation of 4, floored at zero; the population mean is computed from the generated population rather than asserted. Recruitment is weighted sampling without replacement by the exponential-race method, which reduces exactly to simple random sampling when all weights are equal. Convenience and quota weights penalise commuters and job-holders and rise with the person's own study hours, which is selection on the outcome itself; volunteer weights favour first years and heavier studiers; stratified and simple random sampling use equal weights. The non-response dial multiplies every weight by a response probability that falls with commuting and holding a job, and applies to the probability methods too, so a random sample becomes biased once non-response is differential. Response probability enters the weight rather than reducing the achieved sample, which is the equivalent of recruiting until the target is met. The selection weights are invented to make the effect legible and are not measured quantities; real non-response depends on topic, mode, incentive and season and is not one dial. No real institution, register, survey or student is described.

tools.title: Thematic Analysis Coding Laboratory
tools.summary: Six invented interview extracts about asking for help at university, worked one at a time. The learner writes a code of their own, optionally borrows from a bank of six candidate codes that each explain what they do rather than whether they are right, and then sets their reading beside three defensible coding passes over the same words - semantic, latent and situated. Each extract closes with a reflexive prompt about what the reader brought with them. Nothing is scored, and inter-rater agreement is explicitly not the criterion.
learningObjectives: Describe coding in reflexive thematic analysis as an analytic act rather than an extraction.
Produce both semantic and more interpretive codes for the same extract.
State what a given coding decision brings forward and what it pushes out of view.
Distinguish a code from a filing category and from an imported theoretical diagnosis.
Articulate assumptions brought to an extract before coding it.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; anything typed stays in the browser tab, is never compared with anyone else's, and nothing is inferred about the person using the tool.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native text input, select, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. There are no charts: every output is text, so no visual-only information exists to be paired. The extract and the learner's own code are pinned to the top of the stage so the words being coded stay visible while the coding controls beside them are used. Each of the three coding passes names its own level in the heading and prints what it brings forward and what it puts in the background as labelled sentences, so the coloured left border is a redundant cue; each bank code prints its level as text above the label. Progress is shown in a stage track that marks the current and compared extracts with visually hidden text as well as styling. Changes announce full sentences through the polite live region, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Coding as an analytic act: three defensible readings of the same six extracts, and no answer key
tools.simulationNotes: Six short interview extracts invented for teaching, attributed to fictional students of varying year and background, on the topic of asking for help at university. The same fictional dataset is used by the Theme or Topic challenge and the Reflexivity and Alternative Theme Builder in this module, so the three tools can be run as a sequence. Nothing is scored: the tool never marks a code right or wrong and never computes agreement between codings, and the page states why inter-rater agreement is not the criterion for reflexive thematic analysis. Each extract carries a bank of six candidate codes tagged semantic, latent or situated, each with a written note on what that code does and what it costs - including, deliberately, codes that would not survive scrutiny, such as a theoretical construct imported wholesale and a category label that files the extract without saying anything about it. Three coding passes are supplied per extract, chosen to make the semantic-to-situated range visible; they are not the three possibilities, and the debrief says a narrative, psychosocial or feminist reading would produce others. Free text typed by the learner is echoed back without evaluation and is never stored or transmitted.

tools.title: Theme or Topic?
tools.summary: Three clusters of coded extracts from an invented dataset, each with four candidate statements. The learner sorts every candidate into topic summary, useful staging post, developed theme, or beyond what the data can carry, and receives a written note on all four. The three over-reaching candidates fail in three different ways: one asserts a cause, one attributes intent to an institution nobody interviewed, and one imports a construct together with a between-person comparison. A second challenge asks which rewrites would give a weak section a central organising concept.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a topic summary from a developed theme in reflexive thematic analysis.
Name the central organising concept a candidate theme is built around.
Recognise a descriptive statement that is a legitimate stage in an analysis but not yet a theme.
Identify claims that go beyond what interview data can support, and say why in each case.
Rewrite a topic heading so that it carries an analytic claim.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.

tools.title: Sampling Distribution and p-Value Simulator
tools.summary: Two groups of fictional participants are drawn from the same population, so the true difference is exactly zero. Running that study a thousand times builds the sampling distribution of the mean difference, and one observed difference is marked on it with the tails at least that far from zero shaded. The tail area counted in the pile is shown beside the tail area the model predicts. Sample size and variability can be changed, so the same observed difference can be watched moving from p = .5 to p below .001 without the finding changing at all.
learningObjectives: Describe a sampling distribution as the spread of a statistic across repeated studies under a stated model.
Read a p-value off a null distribution as a tail area rather than as a property of the data.

Explain why the same observed difference yields different p-values at different sample sizes.

Tail bars carry a diagonal hatch as well as a different fill, and the observed value is marked with a labelled rule, so the tail area is never carried by colour alone. Four figures - standard error, the observed value in standard errors, the model's tail area and the counted tail area - sit beside the chart in the pinned block. p-values below .001 are reported as such rather than as a spurious third digit. tools.readmeTopic: What a null world looks like: the sampling distribution, the tail area, and everything a p-value is not
tools.simulationNotes: Two groups of n fictional participants are drawn from Normal(0, sigma), so the true difference is exactly zero and the statistic is the difference between the group means. The standard error is sigma times the square root of 2/n and the reference distribution is Normal(0, SE). The reference is normal rather than t because the null model states the population standard deviation, so nothing is estimated from the sample; a real t-test estimates it and pays with heavier tails, which is a later tool in this module and the page says so. The theoretical tail area is twice one minus the standard normal cumulative function of the observed value over the standard error, computed with the Abramowitz and Stegun 26.2.17 approximation; the simulated tail area is a count of how many generated studies reached at least that far from zero, and the two are shown side by side. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals, and changing the model clears the pile because those studies came from a different null world. Nothing in the tool mentions a 0.05 threshold, because whether a tail area of a given size should change anybody's behaviour is a decision rather than a statistical fact. No real study, participant or dataset is involved.

tools.title: Confidence Interval Laboratory
tools.summary: Two staged experiments. In the first, a simulated population has a true mean the studies never see, and repeated samples produce a stack of confidence intervals whose misses are marked, so coverage can be counted rather than asserted; sample size and variability change the width of those intervals and leave the coverage alone. In the second, four fictional trials are judged one at a time against a threshold of practical importance that the learner sets, which makes a precise trivial finding and a wide uninformative one look as different as they are. A select-all challenge then works through the standard misreadings of a 95% interval.
learningObjectives: State what the 95% in a 95% confidence interval is a property of, and why it is not a probability about the interval on screen.
Distinguish the width of an interval from the coverage of the procedure that produced it.
Explain why sample size changes precision but not long-run coverage, and why the confidence level changes both.

tools.readmeTopic: Coverage is a property of the procedure: count the misses, then separate precision from importance
tools.simulationNotes: Experiment 1 draws n observations from Normal(12, sigma) - a fictional mean change of 12.0 minutes of walking per day - and reports the sample mean plus or minus z(level) times sigma over the square root of n, with z taken from a fixed table of normal quantiles at 80, 90, 95 and 99 per cent. Sigma is treated as known because the simulation states it, which is why the multiplier is a normal rather than a t quantile; a real study estimates sigma from its own sample and uses t, which widens the interval at small n, and the page says so in its limitations. Because sigma is known every interval in a run has the same width, so the only thing that varies from study to study is where the interval sits - the picture then shows the intervals moving around a truth that does not. Nominal coverage is exact under this model, so changing n or sigma changes width while only the confidence level changes coverage. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals, and changing any design setting clears the pile because those studies came from a different procedure. Experiment 2 uses four invented trials with fixed reported means and 95% intervals, chosen to occupy the four corners of the precision-by-importance space; the correct classification is computed from the learner's own threshold, so moving the threshold changes the correct verdict without any datum changing.
