tools.title: ANOVA F-Ratio Visualiser
tools.summary: Two staged experiments on the logic of the one-way F ratio. In the first, three simulated groups are drawn from populations whose separation, within-group spread and size the learner controls, and a real ANOVA on the generated sample is shown as a strip plot with each group mean's reach away from the grand mean drawn in; the point is that F responds to both halves of a fraction, and that noise enters as its square. In the second, three visibly different patterns of group means are constructed to have identical between-groups sums of squares, so all three produce F(2, 87) = 7.50 - which is what a significant omnibus test can and cannot tell you.
learningObjectives: Describe F as the ratio of the between-groups mean square to the within-groups mean square.

tools.readmeTopic: F is a fraction: move the signal, move the noise, and meet three patterns of means that share one F
tools.simulationNotes: Experiment 1 draws n observations per group from Normal(52 - s, sigma), Normal(52, sigma) and Normal(52 + s, sigma), where s and sigma are set by sliders, and then runs an actual one-way ANOVA on the generated sample rather than reporting population values: SS between is the sum over groups of n times the squared distance of the group mean from the grand mean, SS within is the pooled sum of squared deviations from each group's own mean, and F is their ratio of mean squares. Tail areas come from the regularised incomplete beta function, evaluated by continued fraction with a Lanczos log-gamma, so p is exact to display precision rather than looked up. The groups are labelled A, B and C on purpose, so that no story about revision does the explaining. Doubling sigma divides the amount by which F exceeds 1 by four, because E[MS between] is sigma squared plus n times the sum of squared population deviations over k minus 1, while E[MS within] is sigma squared; the page states this exactly rather than claiming F itself quarters. Experiment 2 uses three sets of three means - 49/52/55, 50/50/55.196 and 46.804/52/52 - constructed to have identical sums of squared deviations from their own grand means, so at 30 per group and a within-group SD of 6 all three give SS between 540.0 and F(2, 87) = 7.50, p = .001. tools.title: ANCOVA / MANOVA Decision Laboratory
tools.summary: Learners assign a role to every variable in a fictional evaluation before choosing an analysis, then meet two experiments. The first generates eighty students and shows what covariate adjustment does: with random allocation it barely moves the estimate and buys precision instead, with a baseline gap it moves it a long way, and with unequal regression slopes it stops being a single number at all - while a menu switching random allocation for intact classes changes nothing in the arithmetic and everything in the interpretation. The second plots two outcomes at once and compares each on its own with the joint Mahalanobis separation, so that a multivariate test is seen to ask a different question rather than a cheaper one. Four closing scenarios include two whose answer is neither analysis.

Explain that a covariate's main contribution under randomisation is precision rather than correction.

tools.readmeTopic: What a covariate is for, when adjustment misleads, and why MANOVA is not several ANOVAs at once
tools.simulationNotes: Experiment 1 generates two groups of forty. The covariate has mean 50 and standard deviation 10, shifted apart by the group-gap slider; the outcome is 50 plus the group's own slope times the centred covariate, plus half the stated effect in each direction, plus normal noise with standard deviation 10 times the square root of one minus r squared, so that with equal slopes the within-group correlation is r and both variables have standard deviation about 10. Each group's slope is r plus or minus half the slope-difference slider, so the average slope stays at r. The tool then computes, from the generated sample, the unadjusted difference, the pooled within-group slope and the adjusted difference as the unadjusted difference minus that slope times the covariate gap - which is exactly the common-slope ANCOVA adjusted mean difference - together with each group's own slope and the vertical gap between the two fitted lines at three covariate values. The how-groups-were-formed menu changes nothing computational and only what the adjusted number is allowed to mean, which is the honest state of affairs. Experiment 2 draws two standardised outcomes from a bivariate normal with the stated within-group correlation, shifting the group centres by the two standardised differences, and reports the Mahalanobis distance, which equals the square root of (d1 squared minus twice rho d1 d2 plus d2 squared) over one minus rho squared. tools.readmeTopic: A conventionally large effect still leaves two thirds of the two distributions overlapping
tools.simulationNotes: No data are generated: both groups are mathematical normal distributions on an invented 100-point scale, with group A fixed at a mean of 50. The pooled standard deviation is the root mean square of the two group standard deviations, since group sizes are equal, and Cohen's d is the mean difference divided by it. The overlap coefficient is integrated numerically - a trapezoidal sum of the minimum of the two densities over two thousand steps across the plotted range - rather than taken from the closed form 2*Phi(-|d|/2), because that form is only correct when the two standard deviations are equal and this tool deliberately lets them differ. The probability of superiority is Phi of the mean difference over the root of the summed variances, which stays exact under unequal variances, and U3 is defined as the share of group B above group A's mean, Phi of the mean difference over group B's standard deviation. The sample-size slider feeds only a two-sample t statistic, mean difference over pooled SD times the root of two over n on 2n-2 degrees of freedom, with a two-tailed p from the regularised incomplete beta function; at d = 0.80 it runs from t = 1.79, p = .090 at ten per group to t = 11.31, p below .0001 at four hundred, with the effect size and overlap unchanged. Every index describes two distributions and none describes a person, which the page states repeatedly. Cohen's small, medium and large labels are printed with the caveat he attached to them himself.

tools.title: Independent-Samples t-Test: The Null Distribution
tools.summary: The tool works from summary statistics, because that is all a t-test needs, and puts the whole test into one picture: the distribution of t if the two population means were equal, with the tails beyond the observed statistic shaded, the critical values as dashed rules and the standard normal drawn faintly behind so the heavier tails at small degrees of freedom can be seen rather than asserted. Two preset buttons run the same two groups at fifteen and at a hundred per group, so the same finding is read off twice with Cohen's d fixed at 0.50 and p falling from .182 to below .001. A closing challenge asks the learner to choose between four write-ups of one non-significant result.
learningObjectives: Build t from a mean difference and a standard error and place it on the null distribution.
Read a two-tailed p as the area beyond the observed statistic.
Explain why p depends strongly on the sample size while Cohen's d does not.
Explain why the t distribution has heavier tails than the normal and why the gap closes with degrees of freedom.

tools.readmeTopic: One number on one curve: where t comes from, and why p moves with n when d does not
tools.simulationNotes: No data are generated: the tool takes two means, two standard deviations and a sample size and computes the pooled standard deviation as the root mean square of the two group SDs, the standard error as the pooled SD times the square root of two over n, t as the mean difference over that standard error on 2n-2 degrees of freedom, Cohen's d as the mean difference over the pooled SD, and the two-tailed p from the regularised incomplete beta function. Critical values are found by bisection on the tail area, which avoids a separate inverse-t routine and also supplies the confidence interval for the mean difference; the interval excludes zero exactly when the test rejects, and the tool says so. The t density and the standard normal density are both drawn, so the heavier tails at small df are visible rather than asserted. The tool warns when the two standard deviations differ by more than a factor of 1.8, because this is the classic pooled-variance test and Welch's version, which does not assume equal variances, is not computed here. Group sizes are equal throughout. The reference figures a lecturer can check: at fifteen per group with means 50 and 55 and SDs of 10, SE = 3.65, t(28) = 1.37, d = 0.50, p = .182, critical value 2.05; at a hundred per group the same two groups give SE = 1.41, t(198) = 3.54, d = 0.50 and p below .001. All studies, groups and scores are fictional.

tools.title: Statistical Power and Type M Error
tools.summary: Experiment 1 draws the two sampling distributions of the observed effect size - one centred on zero, one on the effect you have assumed - with the rejection threshold between them, so alpha, beta and power become three areas that move when the assumption, the sample size or the threshold moves; a target-power control reports the sample size a planned study would need at each level. Experiment 2 runs two thousand genuinely simulated studies of one real effect and shows both halves of the Type M argument at once: the average of every estimate lands on the truth, and the average of the significant ones is nearly three times it at fifteen per group. A prediction is required before the run.

tools.simulationNotes: In Experiment 1 the observed effect size is treated as approximately normal with standard error the square root of two over n. The rejection threshold uses the exact critical value of t on 2n-2 degrees of freedom converted to the d scale, and the area beyond it is computed from a normal rather than a non-central t; at these sample sizes the difference is a fraction of a percentage point, the page says so in its limitations, and the required sample sizes it produces match published tables - 64 per group for 80% power at d = 0.50 and 253 at d = 0.25, both at alpha .05. Required n is found by scanning upwards until the target is reached. Experiment 2 does not approximate: it generates two thousand real experiments, each drawing two groups of n from Normal(0,1) and Normal(0.35,1), computing the pooled standard deviation, the observed d and the t statistic, and declaring significance when the statistic reaches the exact critical value. At fifteen per group and seed 5477 this gives 301 significant results out of 2000, a mean estimate across all studies of 0.35 - unbiased - a mean among the significant ones of 0.97, an exaggeration ratio of 2.76, and three significant results with the wrong sign; at a hundred and twenty per group the ratio falls to 1.17 and no sign errors remain. tools.title: Correlation: Linearity, Outliers and Shared Variance
tools.summary: Six generated datasets on one frame, with three controls that each carry a lesson: the dataset menu shows a clean curve whose Pearson r is essentially zero, a slider drags one ringed observation towards the corner and swings r from 0.02 to 0.75 in a twelve-point sample while barely moving it in a hundred-and-twenty-point one, and a units menu multiplies y so that the slope moves by a factor of ten and r does not move at all. A disclosure recomputes everything with the ringed point removed. The challenge is an eyeball test: estimate r for three plots on sliders and find out which way your error runs.
learningObjectives: State what Pearson's r does and does not measure.
Interpret r squared as the share of variance accounted for by the straight-line relationship, and say what the remainder is.
Explain why a near-zero correlation is not evidence of no relationship.
Describe how a single observation can dominate r in a small sample.
Distinguish a correlation from a regression slope and explain why one carries units.
interactionTypes: changing the units of the outcome

tools.readmeTopic: r measures straightness, not relatedness: curves, single points and a change of units
tools.simulationNotes: All six datasets are generated by a seeded generator on a 0 to 100 frame, and x and y are deliberately unnamed so that no story does the explaining. The linear sets pair a standard normal x with a y correlated to a stated degree; the curve is a quadratic in x with a small amount of noise, giving a near-perfect relationship and a Pearson r of -0.01. The two odd-point sets use seeds chosen so that the generated cloud has a correlation near zero both with and without the ringed observation - 0.02 across all twelve and 0.08 across the other eleven - which is what makes the pull slider's effect entirely attributable to the one point it moves. Dragging that point to the corner takes r to 0.75 in the twelve-point set and to 0.04 in the hundred-and-twenty-point set. The units menu multiplies every y value by a constant, so the slope moves by exactly that factor - 0.87 becomes 8.69 or 0.17 - and r stays at 0.85, because the slope is r times the ratio of the standard deviations and therefore carries units. The challenge plots have correlations of 0.29, 0.86 and -0.63, and the feedback names the systematic underestimation of strong correlations rather than simply scoring the answers. Nothing here is real data, and no correlation on the page could establish causation.

tools.title: Regression: Intercept, Slope and Least Squares
tools.summary: Thirty generated observations and a line the learner moves by hand. Every residual is drawn, optionally as the literal square whose area is being minimised, and the sum of squared errors updates live against a goal banner; a reveal then shows the least-squares solution, which no amount of dragging beats. The region outside the observed range of x is shaded, so the intercept can be seen to be a prediction for somebody who does not exist, and a disclosure shows the identical fit with x centred on its mean - same slope, same predictions, same residuals, and an intercept that finally describes a real part of the data. The challenge asks for one interpolated prediction, one extrapolated one, and a decision about which to report.
learningObjectives: Define a residual as an observation minus a prediction.
Explain what the least-squares criterion minimises and why no other line can do better.
Interpret a slope and an intercept in the units of the study.
Explain when an intercept is mathematically necessary and substantively empty, and what centring does about it.
Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation and say what R squared does and does not tell you.
interactionTypes: hand-fitting a line against a live error total
numeric prediction challenge with a judgement

tools.readmeTopic: Try to beat the least-squares line, then find out what the intercept is a prediction for
tools.simulationNotes: Thirty observations are generated from a seeded generator: x is uniform between 12 and 68 minutes and y is 30 plus 0.6 times x plus normal noise with a standard deviation of 7. The least-squares solution is written down directly - the slope is the covariance of x and y over the variance of x, the intercept is whatever puts the line through the point of means - rather than searched for, so the reveal is an answer and not a better guess. At seed 2884 the fitted line is a predicted score of 27.7 plus 0.68 times minutes, with a squared error total of 1399 and 71.5 per cent of the variance accounted for; the mean of x is 35.9 minutes and the mean of y is 52.3 points, so the mean-centred parameterisation has the same slope, the same predictions of 48.2 at thirty minutes and 65.3 at fifty-five, the same error total, and an intercept of 52.3 instead of 27.7. R squared is reported for the candidate line as well and is allowed to go negative, because a line worse than predicting the mean of y for everybody is exactly what a negative value means. No standard errors or confidence intervals are computed, and the assumptions behind least squares are not checked - that is the following tool in this module. Nothing here is real data, and the slope is a comparison between people rather than a statement about changing anybody.

tools.title: Homoscedasticity and Residual Diagnostics
tools.summary: One generated dataset drawn twice on a shared fitted-value axis - the raw scatterplot above, residuals against fitted values below - so that a variance pattern which is arguable in the first is unmistakable in the second. Five patterns of residual spread can be dialled from flat to severe, and the estimated slope keeps landing on the true 0.50 while the standard error stops being trustworthy. A disclosure reports the exact standard error the generating model implies beside the one the classical formula is aiming at, and confirms it with the coverage of both intervals across four hundred repeated samples. The challenge is four residual plots to read, one of which is not about variance at all and one of which cannot honestly be diagnosed.
learningObjectives: Define homoscedasticity as approximately constant conditional residual variance.
Read a residuals-against-fitted-values plot, and explain why the horizontal axis must be fitted values rather than the outcome.
Explain why non-constant variance leaves the slope estimate unbiased while making its standard error untrustworthy.
Explain why the size and direction of that error depend on where the extra spread sits relative to the extremes of the predictor.
Treat a residual plot as a fallible diagnostic rather than a verdict, and say why a formal test does not settle it either.
interactionTypes: two linked views of one dataset
continuous manipulation of variance pattern and severity
residual spread compared across three regions

tools.readmeTopic: The residual plot is the instrument: what non-constant variance does to the standard error, and what it leaves alone
tools.simulationNotes: Observations are generated with x uniform on 10 to 90 and y = 20 + 0.5x plus normal noise whose standard deviation is 5 times a shape factor. The factor is 1 for constant variance and otherwise ramps to six times at severity 100 per cent, in one of four shapes: growing with x, shrinking with x, widest at both extremes, or widest in the middle. The last two exist because they are what makes the lesson honest: the classical standard error goes wrong to the extent that the variance lines up with leverage, which is largest at both extremes of x. Measured over 3,000 samples at n = 120 and full severity, the coverage of a nominal 95 per cent classical interval is 94.7 per cent for constant variance, 92.5 per cent for a megaphone, 86.0 per cent for variance at both extremes and 99.5 per cent - conservative rather than liberal - for variance in the middle, while the robust HC3 interval stays between 93.8 and 94.8 per cent throughout and the mean estimated slope is within 0.005 of 0.500 in every case. The tool's wording is generated from an exact model-based quantity rather than from the shape or from the simulated coverage: it computes the true standard error of the slope from the known sigma at each x and compares it with the value the classical formula is aiming at, giving ratios of 1.00, 1.05, 1.28 and 0.68 for the four patterns at full severity. The simulated coverage is reported alongside as confirmation, with its Monte Carlo error stated. No formal test for non-constant variance is computed; Breusch-Pagan and White's test are named in the page and deliberately absent, because a test invites the discussion to collapse into a threshold and because such tests are themselves sensitive to sample size. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. No real study or dataset is involved.

tools.title: Multiple Comparisons, FWER and Forking Paths
tools.summary: Experiment 1 runs a family of real two-sample t-tests in which every null is true, draws one square per test with the significant ones crossed, and sets the counted family-wise error rate beside 1 minus (1 minus alpha) to the power k; a Bonferroni option then shows the false-positive rate collapse and, in the same readout, the detection rate for the real effects collapsing with it. Experiment 2 generates ninety fictional students with no group difference on anything and offers four outcomes, three exclusion rules, three subgroups and two covariate decisions - seventy-two complete, defensible analyses of the same empty data - and lets the learner search until something reaches p below .05, then reveals how many other paths would have done the same. A closing challenge separates planned multiplicity, exploratory analysis, undisclosed selective reporting and confirmatory inference.

Describe what a Bonferroni correction buys and what it costs, in the same breath.
Explain how ordinary analytic flexibility inflates false positives without anyone intending to cheat.
Explain why a reported p-value assumes it was the only analysis run.

tools.readmeTopic: Why flexibility inflates false positives without anyone cheating, and what a correction costs
tools.simulationNotes: Experiment 1 runs k genuine two-sample t-tests on 40 per group rather than drawing p-values from a uniform, so the grid on screen is an actual analysis; a chosen number of the tests carry a real effect of d = 0.60 and the rest have nothing to find. At k = 20 and alpha .05 the predicted family-wise rate is 64.2 per cent and a thousand simulated experiments give 63.0 per cent, with 1.00 predicted false positives per experiment against 0.98 counted. With five real effects among the twenty and no correction, 53.2 per cent of experiments produce at least one false positive and 75.6 per cent of the real effects are detected; switching Bonferroni on takes the threshold to .0025, the family-wise rate to 3.9 per cent counted against 4.9 predicted, and the detection rate down to 33.9 per cent - the trade is deliberately shown in one readout. Experiment 2 generates ninety fictional students, half in each group, with four correlated outcomes, a baseline test, a response-speed measure and a cohort label, and with no group difference on anything; each of the 72 paths filters the rows by exclusion rule and subgroup, optionally residualises the outcome on the baseline score, and runs a pooled two-sample t-test, so the paths are heavily correlated exactly as a real analyst's would be and no simple correction applies. On the default dataset five of the 72 reach p below .05 and the smallest is p = .026, and every one of those is a false positive by construction. The tool never presents the search as a technique: the goal banner and the feedback both say that it is a demonstration of what searching does to the meaning of the resulting p-value, and that every choice offered is one a careful researcher might make in good faith. tools.title: Double Dissociation Detective
tools.summary: Six fictional case files, each giving one or two people, two tasks and a fictional control group for every task. Students return a verdict on each file - not enough evidence, a general severity difference, a single dissociation, a double dissociation, or a crossover the tasks cannot support - and receive feedback built from the numbers rather than from a stored answer key. One file has a 58-point raw gap that disappears once each score is read against its own controls; another changes verdict as a test-length slider moves without a single score changing.

Explain why a crossover rules out task difficulty as an explanation, and what it leaves open.
Reference a score to its own control group rather than comparing raw percentages across tasks.
Judge whether a difference is larger than the measurement precision of the test that produced it.
Identify task impurity in a case where a real crossover fails to isolate the process of interest.

tools.readmeTopic: Single and double dissociations: what a crossover rules out, what measurement precision permits, and where task impurity defeats both
tools.simulationNotes: Six invented case files with invented people, tasks and control groups. Every score is referenced to its own control group as z = (score - control mean) / control SD. Precision is modelled with a binomial standard error, SE = sqrt(p(1-p)/n) divided by the control SD, and a within-person difference counts as resolvable when it exceeds 1.96 times the standard error of the difference. Classification follows the logic rather than the size of the gap: no resolvable difference gives insufficient evidence, one gives a single dissociation, two in the same direction give a general severity difference, two in opposite directions give a double dissociation, and a case flagged as task-impure gives a confounded crossover. Deliberate simplifications: the observed proportion is held fixed while test length varies so the slider isolates precision; control mean and SD are treated as known exactly, whereas proper single-case comparison uses a modified t test and gives wider intervals; and the binomial error assumes independent, equally difficult items. Reference values at the default 40 items per task - case 1 difference 4.75 SD against 2.63 needed, case 2 2.38 and 2.62 against 1.79 and 1.73, case 3 6.52 and 4.07 against 2.43 and 1.78, case 4 0.18 against 2.16, case 5 1.70 and 1.80 against 1.97 and 1.94, case 6 4.47 and 6.07 against 2.14 and 2.83. No real person, published case, clinical instrument or norm is reproduced, and nothing on the page diagnoses, assesses or gives a prognosis for anybody.

tools.readmeTopic: Why 'damage here, difficulty there' is not 'this region does that': lesion extent, vascular territory, diaschisis, premorbid level, co-occurring damage and task demands
tools.simulationNotes: One invented case with an invented history, an invented scan and invented testing. The confidence ceiling is a teaching device rather than a calculation: it encodes the judgement that a single case with a large multi-region lesion inside a systematic vascular territory, measured at two weeks, in a person of unknown premorbid level and possibly atypical language organisation, cannot carry a general claim about what a region does. No real patient, published case or clinical record is described, and nothing on the page diagnoses anybody or offers a prognosis.

tools.title: Network Disconnection Mapper
tools.summary: A deliberately simplified fictional network of five regions and six pathways, with four tasks that each need a particular route through it. Students damage a region or cut a pathway and watch which tasks notice. Two tasks have a weaker second route, so some damage makes them effortful and error-prone rather than impossible, and several different single failures turn out to produce exactly the same behavioural profile.
learningObjectives: Explain how a task can fail while every region involved is undamaged.
Identify several different points of network failure that produce identical behaviour.
Distinguish a task that fails from a task running on a weaker second route.
State why a symptom constrains where a network has failed without identifying it.
Explain why localisation and network accounts are complementary rather than rival.
topics: many-to-one mapping of symptoms to causes
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native checkbox, radio and button controls; every element of the network is toggled by a labelled checkbox rather than by clicking the diagram, so the whole tool is keyboard operable. The diagram is planar by construction, so no two pathways cross. It is hidden from assistive technology and paired with two visible tables: one giving each task, the state of its main and second routes and the outcome, and one giving every region and pathway with its current state. Damage is carried by a broken outline and a printed cross, never by fill alone; task outcomes are carried by the words Normal, Impaired and Fails as well as by a left border. Changes announce through the shell's polite live region with a full four-task summary. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers; the pinned primary is 361px at 1366x768 so the diagram and the four outcomes stay visible while the pathway checkboxes at the bottom of the control column are reached. Heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Disconnection: why a deficit can follow from a cut pathway between intact regions, and why the same profile can have several different causes
tools.simulationNotes: An invented network of five regions (seeing objects, meaning, word sounds, speech output, hearing speech) and six pathways. Each of four tasks is defined as an ordered route of regions and pathways that must all be intact; two tasks also have a second, weaker route. The outcome is normal when the main route is complete, impaired when only the second route is complete, and a failure otherwise. Three single failures - damaging the word-sound store, damaging the speech-output region, and cutting the pathway between them - produce identical outcomes on all four tasks, which is the point of the challenge. Cutting the direct picture-to-word pathway affects none of the four tasks, which is the point of the damage-without-deficit branch. Deliberate simplifications: real connections are partially damaged rather than cut, real regions belong to many networks at once, and three outcome states stand in for a continuum. The names describe jobs rather than anatomy, the positions carry no anatomical meaning, no real region, tract, connectome or published model is reproduced, and no syndrome is named anywhere in the tool.

tools.title: Visual Neglect Laboratory
tools.summary: Line bisection, cancellation and copying a scene, run on five fictional profiles: no difficulty, left neglect organised around the viewer, left neglect organised around each object, left visual field loss without neglect, and both together. An examiner prompt can be switched on and off. The copying task separates neglect from field loss cleanly, and separates the two kinds of neglect from each other.
learningObjectives: Explain why unilateral neglect is not blindness on one side.
Name the task signatures that separate neglect from visual field loss, including the opposite directions of the bisection error.
Distinguish neglect organised around the viewer from neglect organised around each object.
Explain what an examiner prompt does and does not fix, and why.
Say why neglect cannot be assigned to one brain region.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it. Nobody is tested and nothing here can assess anybody.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radio, checkbox and button controls; the drawings are display-only and nothing has to be clicked or dragged inside them. Each drawing is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a readout giving the headline result, the prompt state and the unprompted-to-prompted change, plus two tables: one breaking the current result down by line, by third of the page or by object in the scene, and one giving every profile's result on the current task with and without the prompt. Nothing carries meaning by colour: a bisection mark is a tall stroke and the true middle a short notch, a found star carries a stroke through it while a missed one does not, and an omitted part of a copy is simply absent. Every change announces a full summary through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Neglect against field loss, and viewer-centred against object-centred neglect: the task signatures that separate them and what cueing fixes
tools.simulationNotes: Five fictional profiles, each a rule rather than a person, and three original tasks. Bisection deviation is a fraction of line length, positive rightward: viewer-centred neglect uses 0.06 plus 0.16 times one minus the line's position across the page, so the error grows for lines further left; object-centred neglect uses a constant 0.13 wherever the line sits; field loss uses a constant minus 0.05, towards the blind side. Cancellation uses a logistic in horizontal position drawn against a fixed seed (mulberry32, seed 20260807), with a steep function at the page edge for field loss rather than a gradient. Copying drops parts by page position for viewer-centred neglect and by side-within-object for object-centred neglect. The prompt multiplies the neglect component by 0.55, moves the viewer-centred copy cut-off leftwards, removes the field-loss effect entirely, and does nothing at all to object-centred copying because it is an instruction about the page. Reference values at the default settings - bisection means: no difficulty plus 0.3 per cent, viewer-centred neglect plus 14.0 per cent (18.4, 14.0 and 9.6 across the three lines), object-centred neglect plus 13.0 per cent on every line, field loss minus 5.0 per cent, both plus 8.9 per cent. Cancellation out of 26, unprompted then prompted: 26 and 26, 15 and 18, 19 and 24, 24 and 26, 14 and 18. Copying out of 19: 19 and 19, 10 and 13, 12 and 12, 19 and 19, 10 and 13. No clinical instrument is reproduced, no scoring is clinical, no real person is described, and nothing here diagnoses, assesses or gives a prognosis for anybody.

tools.title: Visual Field Defect Mapper
tools.summary: Six points on a schematic visual pathway - optic nerve, chiasm, tract, the two halves of the radiation, and occipital cortex. For each, the learner ticks which quadrants of which eye's field they expect to go dark before revealing the textbook mapping, and is marked cell by cell. The challenge runs the inference backwards: given a complete homonymous defect, which points on the pathway are compatible? Four of eight are.
learningObjectives: Predict the field consequence of damage in front of, at and behind the optic chiasm.
Explain why only half the fibres crossing is what makes a field pattern informative.
Distinguish a defect confined to one eye from one that respects the vertical midline in both.
State which parts of the pathway a field pattern can identify and which it cannot.
Explain why quadrant diagrams are a teaching fiction rather than a picture of a real field examination.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. Nothing on the page examines anybody's vision and no result means anything about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radio, checkbox and button controls throughout; the eight prediction checkboxes sit in two two-by-two grids to keep the control column short while each target keeps its full 2.75rem height. Both graphics are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables: a quadrant-by-quadrant table giving what the learner predicted and what the mapping gives for all eight cells, and a summary table of every point on the pathway. Nothing depends on colour: a lost quadrant carries a printed cross as well as a fill, a predicted quadrant carries a dot, the damage marker is a circled cross, the crossing fibres at the chiasm are dashed, and the two sides of the brain are labelled L and R. Reveals and site changes announce through the shell's polite live region. Changing a prediction after a reveal withdraws the reveal, so the marking can never be stale. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Predicting field loss from a point on the visual pathway - and finding out how little the pattern can say in reverse
tools.simulationNotes: Idealised textbook mappings on a schematic pathway. Field quadrants are coded per eye as upper-left, lower-left, upper-right and lower-right of that eye's own field. Left optic nerve gives the whole left eye; the centre of the chiasm gives the outer half of each eye; the right optic tract, both halves of the right radiation together, and the right occipital cortex each give the left half of both fields, with the occipital case drawn with the centre spared. The right temporal radiation gives the upper-left quadrant in both eyes and the right parietal radiation the lower-left. Two of the six rows are identical in quadrant terms, which is the point of the reverse-inference challenge: four of its eight options are compatible with a complete left homonymous defect. Deliberate simplifications: quadrants are a teaching fiction, since real defects have soft edges, vary in depth rather than being present or absent, and rarely respect a quadrant boundary; real lesions are partial and produce incomplete and asymmetric defects far more often than tidy ones; macular sparing is included because every textbook includes it, and the tool states that its explanation is still argued about. The diagram is schematic, nothing is to scale, no real perimetry, image or clinical instrument is reproduced, no cause is named, and nothing on the page examines or diagnoses anybody.

tools.title: Memory Systems Detective
tools.summary: Five fictional memory profiles across seven control-referenced measures, and five claims about separable memory systems. For every claim on every profile the learner decides whether the profile supports it, counts against it, or cannot decide it, and receives an explanation built from that profile's own numbers. Of the twenty-five cells, twelve cannot be decided - and the retrieval-versus-storage claim is never supported anywhere.
learningObjectives: State what a profile must contain before it supports a distinction between memory systems.
Distinguish the claim that two tasks are separable from the claim that two systems exist.
Explain why normal recognition with impaired recall does not establish a retrieval account.
Identify task impurity in a profile where every impaired measure shares its material.
List the non-neurological explanations of a uniformly slightly-below-average profile.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radio and button controls throughout. The profile chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving every measure, what it asks the person to do, the distance from its own control group and its standing in words. Every bar also prints its own value, so the fill is redundant, and bars clearly outside the control range are distinguished by fill and by a wording in the table rather than by colour alone. The claim under judgement sits in a goal banner in the interactive header, so it is readable while the verdict radios at the bottom of the control column are used, and the profile chart is pinned at 294px so the evidence stays on screen. Grid cells print the verdict as a word and add the intended verdict when they differ. Every judgement announces through the shell's polite live region with a running count. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: When a memory profile supports a distinction between systems, when it counts against one, and the twelve times out of twenty-five that it cannot decide
tools.simulationNotes: Five invented profiles with invented numbers on seven invented measures, each expressed as a distance from the average of that measure's own fictional control group in control standard deviations. A measure counts as clearly below its controls at minus two or lower and as within range above about minus 1.2. The intended grid, rows being the five claims and columns profiles A to E: short-term against episodic gives support, support, support, cannot, cannot; episodic against semantic gives support, cannot, support, cannot, cannot; episodic against skill gives support, cannot, support, cannot, cannot; retrieval against storage gives cannot in all five; and one general reduction gives against, against, against, against, support. Eight cells support a claim, five count against one, and twelve cannot decide. The retrieval row is never supported anywhere, deliberately: the pattern always cited for it - recall at floor with normal recognition - does not establish it, because recognition is the easier task and a trace too weak to be recalled can still be strong enough to be recognised. Deliberate simplifications: seven measures is very few, real batteries separate several things merged here, and the intended answers are judgements the tool invites the learner to argue with. No anatomy appears anywhere, because these distinctions are between what tasks require. No real person, published case, clinical instrument or syndrome name is used, and nothing on the page diagnoses anybody or offers a prognosis.

tools.title: Aphasia Profile Comparator
tools.summary: Six fictional language profiles on six original measures - fluency of spontaneous speech, understanding, repetition, naming, reading aloud and writing. The learner puts any two side by side, predicts which single measure does most to separate them, and is marked against the arithmetic. One profile fits no textbook pattern, which is the subject of the challenge.
learningObjectives: Identify which measure carries the most information about a particular contrast.
Explain why repetition is disproportionately informative, and what a disproportionate difficulty or sparing implies.
Recognise when two measures separate a pair so nearly equally that the largest gap is not a useful answer.
Explain why the classical categories fit a substantial minority of people badly.
State why a language profile constrains the processing more tightly than it constrains the anatomy.
interactionTypes: prediction of the most separating measure
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native select, radio and button controls. The paired bar chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving each measure, what it asks for, both scores and the separation, with the largest separation named in words in its own cell. The two profiles are distinguished by fill and by the profile letter printed at the start of each bar, and every bar prints its own score, so nothing depends on hue. A second table gives all six profiles on all six measures with the selected pair marked. The chart is pinned at 358px so both profiles stay visible while the measure radios at the bottom of the control column are used. Selecting a pair and checking a choice both announce through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Which piece of language evidence separates two profiles, why repetition is disproportionately informative, and why the classical categories are prototypes
tools.simulationNotes: Six invented profiles on six invented measures, scored 0 to 10 where 10 is performance indistinguishable from a fictional control group. The separation between two profiles on a measure is the absolute difference between their scores, and the most informative measure for a pair is the one with the largest separation; measures within one point of the largest are reported as a near tie, because the largest gap stops being a useful answer at that point. Reference pairs - profile A against profile D is separated by repetition alone, by five points, with every other separation one point or less; profile A against profile B has fluency at seven and understanding at six, a near tie; profile C against profile D has repetition at six and fluency at five; profile B against profile C is separated by understanding, by six. Profile F fits no textbook pattern deliberately. Deliberate simplifications: six measures is a caricature, since real assessment separates single-word from sentence comprehension, word from non-word repetition and regular from irregular reading; fluency in particular bundles rate, phrase length, effort, articulation, grammatical structure and information content into one number. No standardised battery, subtest or item is reproduced, the task descriptions are original, no syndrome is named anywhere, no real person or published case appears, and nothing on the page assesses or diagnoses anybody.

tools.title: Executive Function Task Laboratory
tools.summary: Two staged experiments on four original executive tasks and six capacities. In the first, learners predict which processes each task requires and then reveal the model's weights - no task loads on fewer than five of the six. In the second, six capacity sliders and a strategy slider show that reducing inhibition and reducing processing speed both make the colour-word task the lowest score, and that a summary score can hide a complete reversal of the speed-accuracy trade-off.
learningObjectives: Explain why every executive task requires several processes at once.
Show that the mapping from a lowest task score to a reduced capacity is many-to-one.
Explain why processing speed and sustained effort must be accounted for before any executive interpretation.
Describe what a single summary score hides about a speed-accuracy trade-off.
State why 'executive function' is a description of a set of demands rather than a mechanism.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it. Nobody performs the tasks and no score means anything about the reader.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radio, checkbox, range and button controls; the capacity sliders announce meaningful values such as 'Inhibition at 35 per cent of the typical level' and the strategy slider announces 'leaning towards speed'. Each experiment has its own pinned primary chart and the inactive one is hidden, so only one primary is ever visible. Both charts are hidden from assistive technology and each carries a visible sentence inside its own figure stating the same information in words - every weight and every capacity ticked in experiment 1, every score and the lowest task in experiment 2 - because the pinned chart stays on screen while the tables scroll away. Each chart is also paired with a visible table: in experiment 1 a prediction-against-model table for every capacity, in experiment 2 a table giving each task's summary score with accuracy and speed shown separately for the timed tasks. The learner's prediction is drawn as a tick shape rather than a colour and repeated as yes or no in the table; every bar prints its own number; the lowest task is named in the interpretation as well as filled differently. A stage track marks progress. All changes announce through the shell's polite live region. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, reduced motion and forced colours are handled, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Why no executive task is pure, why a low score identifies nothing on its own, and what a summary score hides about strategy
tools.simulationNotes: Four invented tasks and six invented capacities. Each task is a set of weights on the capacities; each capacity has a level between 0 and 1 where 1 is typical; the simulated score is 100 times the weighted sum of levels over the sum of weights, so all capacities at 1 give 100 on every task. The weight matrix - inhibition, switching, updating, planning, speed, effort - is 0.90, 0.10, 0.15, 0, 0.70, 0.50 for the colour-word task; 0.50, 0.90, 0.40, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50 for the rule-change task; 0.30, 0.10, 0.90, 0, 0.50, 0.60 for the running-total task; and 0.50, 0.20, 0.60, 0.90, 0.15, 0.40 for the disc puzzle. No row has fewer than five non-zero weights. Reference values with a single capacity reduced to 0.35 and the rest typical, in task order - reduced inhibition gives 75, 88, 92, 88; reduced processing speed gives 81, 93, 86, 96; reduced updating gives 96, 91, 76, 86; reduced sustained effort gives 86, 88, 84, 91. Reduced inhibition and reduced speed both make the colour-word task the lowest; reduced updating and reduced effort both make the running-total task the lowest; the tool computes this rather than asserting it. The strategy slider splits the summary score of the two timed tasks into accuracy minus 12s and speed plus 12s, where s runs from minus one to plus one, so the summary score itself never moves. Deliberate simplifications: the weights are an argument about task demands rather than measured loadings, six capacities is fewer than the literature separates, and a weighted average has no thresholds, floor or ceiling effects or interactions. Nobody performs the tasks, no standardised test, subtest or item is reproduced, and no anatomy is mentioned anywhere.

tools.title: Split-Brain Laboratory
tools.summary: Two staged experiments about the logic of a lateralised trial. In the first, learners build a trial - item, visual field, response channel, corpus callosum - commit to a prediction and run it, until they have found a combination the section changes and one it does not. In the second, the trial that classically fails is fixed and the five conditions it depends on can be switched off one at a time, turning a famous finding into an ordinary one. Nothing is presented to a visual field; the tool reports what a deliberately simplified routing model gives.
learningObjectives: Work out, for any combination of visual field and response channel, whether a disconnected hemisphere can answer.
Explain why the split-brain findings are a statement about routing rather than about what each hemisphere is for.
Name at least three methodological conditions that would make the classic demonstration stop working.
Distinguish a result that challenges an account from a result produced by a procedural failure.
State why split-brain evidence does not support left-brained or right-brained descriptions of people.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. Nothing is presented to the reader's visual field and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native select, radio, checkbox and button controls throughout, each with an accessible name. The routing diagram is hidden from assistive technology and carries a visible sentence inside its own figure naming the item, the receiving hemisphere, the channel asked with, the state of the callosum and the outcome - the diagram is pinned while the tables scroll away, so the pin reads on its own. Nothing in the drawing is carried by colour: the active route is a thick solid line against thin dashed ones, active boxes carry a heavier border and their own label text, and the section is drawn as a cross over a gap as well as being named. Each experiment has its own pinned primary and the inactive one is hidden, so only one is ever visible; measured heights at 1366 by 768 are 419px for experiment 1 and 229px for experiment 2. The condition explanations of experiment 2 sit outside the pinned block so that the pin cannot grow past its budget. A live goal checklist writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' into the text rather than relying on the marker. Every trial, preset and condition change announces through the shell's polite live region, and focus moves to the laboratory heading when the prediction unlocks it. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, forced colours are handled, and there is no horizontal page scroll at 320px, 375px, 1366px, 1440px or 1920px.
tools.readmeTopic: Why the split-brain findings are about routing rather than about what each hemisphere is for, and what the classic demonstration quietly depends on
tools.simulationNotes: A deliberately simplified routing model, stated as such on the page. Each visual field projects to the opposite hemisphere; each hand is controlled by the opposite hemisphere; speech is produced by the left hemisphere; with the callosum intact whatever one hemisphere receives is available to the other; after a complete section a response succeeds only when the hemisphere that received the item also controls the channel asked with. That gives twelve combinations: all twelve succeed with the callosum intact, and after a section the three that succeed are right field with speech, right field with the right hand, and left field with the left hand. Experiment 2 fixes the trial at left field, spoken report, complete section and lists five conditions it depends on - brief presentation, monitored fixation, a complete section including the splenium, controlled cross-cueing, and left-only speech in this individual. Losing fixation monitoring makes the trial uninterpretable; breaking any of the other four lets the word be reported without disturbing the routing account. Deliberate simplifications: nothing is presented to a visual field because a browser cannot control fixation or duration, real performance varies with material, task, interval, practice and individual, speech is not left-lateralised in everyone, and many disconnected right hemispheres read simple words. The four items are ordinary words invented for this page; no published stimulus, image or procedure is reproduced and no real participant appears.

tools.title: Face Recognition Detective
tools.summary: A six-component model of recognising a person, with a face route and a voice route that converge. In the first experiment learners place a difficulty at one component and read the profile of seven task outcomes it produces. In the second they work backwards from six invented profiles - one of which fits two components because the control task was not administered, and one of which fits none at all - and receive the alternative explanations that come before any component.
learningObjectives: Say what each of six components contributes to recognising a person.
Read a profile of task outcomes backwards to the component that would explain it.
Use the voice route to decide whether a difficulty is confined to faces.
Recognise when a profile is compatible with more than one component, or with none.
List the explanations that come before any face-system account of a low score.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. There is no self-test and no score for the reader, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radio, select and button controls, each with an accessible name (verified programmatically). The flow diagram is hidden from assistive technology and carries a visible sentence inside its own figure naming the affected component and what it does to each route; the affected box is crossed through and labelled 'affected' as well as being filled differently. The seven task outcomes are a list in which every item prints its own word - 'within range', 'impaired' or 'not administered' - so the left border is never the only carrier, and mismatches are marked with an attribute as well as a tint. A full table gives each task, what it asks for, the components it needs and its outcome. Each experiment has its own pinned primary and the inactive one is hidden; measured at 1366 by 768 the pins are 517px and 246px, and with the last control of either experiment scrolled to the bottom of the window the primary is still on screen. The schematic faces are decorative in the strict sense - nothing in the model depends on them - and are marked aria-hidden with their explanation in adjacent text. A live goal checklist writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' into the text. Every change announces through the shell's polite live region and focus moves to the model heading when the prediction unlocks it. Heading levels do not skip, forced colours are handled, and there is no horizontal page scroll at 320px, 375px, 1366px, 1440px or 1920px.
tools.readmeTopic: Why recognising someone is several separable steps, how a voice task decides whether a difficulty is about faces, and when a profile has no answer
tools.simulationNotes: Six components - general visual processing, face perception, face familiarity, voice recognition, person identity knowledge and name retrieval - arranged as two routes that converge on person identity knowledge and then on name retrieval. Seven tasks, each listing the components it needs: object discrimination needs general vision; face discrimination adds face perception; face familiarity adds familiarity; identity from the face adds person identity; name from the face adds name retrieval; identity from the voice needs voice recognition and person identity; name from the voice adds name retrieval. A task is impaired exactly when the affected component is one it needs. The model is all-or-nothing on purpose: it is a device for reasoning about patterns, not a simulation of severity. Six invented profiles: A fits face perception uniquely, B fits face familiarity, C fits person identity knowledge, D fits name retrieval, E fits nothing because every task is below range and any single component leaves something intact, and F fits both general visual processing and face perception because the non-face control task was not administered. The tool searches all six locations rather than asserting any of this. Schematic faces are generated from seven numbers - head width, chin width, eye spacing, eye height, eye size, nose length, mouth width - by mulberry32 from a visible seed starting at 20260807 and advancing by 1013 on each redraw. Deliberate simplifications: six components is fewer than the literature separates, whether familiarity is a stage at all is argued about, there is no severity, no day-to-day variation and no compensation from hair, gait, context or clothing. No published case, clinical measure or photograph is used, no anatomy is named, and nothing on the page assesses the reader.

tools.title: Assessment Battery Builder
tools.summary: Three fictional referrals, a ninety-minute session and seventeen generically described task types. Learners tick tasks and watch four checks update live - converging evidence on the referral question, a domain expected to be intact, the context measures that referral needs, and whether the battery fits the session. Submitting produces a verdict in two halves: what the battery could say and what it could not. The tool evaluates the design of a battery and never scores a person.
learningObjectives: Select assessment tasks from a referral question rather than from a list of respected tests.
Explain why two measures of the same demand say more than one.
Say why a battery needs a domain the referral does not ask about.
Name the measures that answer no referral question and without which nothing else can be interpreted.
Treat session time as a design constraint rather than an administrative detail.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. No score is produced for anybody, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native checkbox, select and button controls, each with an accessible name (verified programmatically). Every task label carries its own duration, so the time cost is readable without consulting the chart. The session-time bar is hidden from assistive technology and paired, inside its own figure, with a sentence stating the number of tasks, the minutes used, the budget and whether the battery is deliverable; the end of the session is drawn as a dashed line and named in the axis text. The four checks are a list in which each item writes '(met)' or '(not yet)' into its own text, so the marker is never the only carrier. The control column is a bank of seventeen checkboxes, which is why the primary is pinned - measured at 1366 by 768 the pinned block is 272 to 293px depending on how much is selected and with the submit button scrolled to the bottom of the window the checks are still at the top of the stage. Every selection, preset and submission announces through the shell's polite live region, and focus moves to the builder heading when the prediction unlocks it. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, forced colours are handled, and there is no horizontal page scroll at 320px, 375px, 1366px, 1440px or 1920px.
tools.readmeTopic: Why a battery is chosen from the referral question, and why the measures that answer no question at all are the ones that make the rest interpretable
tools.simulationNotes: Seventeen generically described task types across attention, memory, language, executive, visuospatial and context, with round teaching durations totalling 167 minutes against a 90-minute session budget. The tool evaluates the design of a battery, never a person, on four checks: converging evidence (at least two tasks in the referral's target domains and at least one in each of them); a comparison domain (at least one task in a domain the referral does not ask about); the two context measures that referral names; and total time within the budget. Two softer signals sit alongside: a burden warning above 70 minutes, and a redundancy note when two selected tasks share a narrow measure outside the target domains. One dependency is modelled - recognition of a word list cannot be administered without the learning task that produced it - and a task with an unmet dependency counts towards nothing. The three referrals target language (context: premorbid estimate and sensory screen), memory with attention (context: mood and effort), and visuospatial with memory (context: sensory screen and mood); each has a worked battery of 50, 58 and 65 minutes respectively that meets all four checks. Deliberate simplifications: task descriptions are generic and no published test, subtest, item, stimulus, norm or administration time is reproduced; four checks is a caricature of a real selection, which also weighs language, literacy, education, cultural background, sensory and motor limitations, whether appropriate norms exist and what the person wants from the assessment; assessment is not a task list, and history, interview, informant report, observation and formulation appear nowhere; and the domains are a convenience because every task loads on several. No anatomy, no diagnosis, no prognosis.

tools.title: Recovery and Plasticity Simulator
tools.summary: Two staged experiments on what a rising score after an injury can establish. The first draws five simulated people over twenty-four months with individual variation and measurement noise, so there is no single recovery curve. The second takes one trained score apart into starting capacity, restitution, relearning, compensation and practice, and compares it with a task the person has never practised - two preset routes reach the same trained score of 86 with untrained scores of 80 and 71.
learningObjectives: Name four processes that all raise a score after an injury and say how they differ.
Explain why a single trained-task score cannot separate them.
State what an untrained task, an alternate test form and an untreated comparison group each rule out.
Read a fan of trajectories rather than a single curve, and judge whether a month-to-month change means anything.
Explain why compensation is a real gain and still not restored function.
interactionTypes: presets that converge on the same score
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; everything runs in the browser tab. Nothing here is a prognosis and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native range, radio and button controls, each with an accessible name; every slider carries a meaningful aria-valuetext in words, such as 'Injury severity 5 of 10, moderate, starting capacity 55 points' and '9 months after the injury'. All three charts are hidden from assistive technology and each carries a visible sentence inside its own figure giving the same information in numbers, and each is paired with a table. Nothing depends on colour: the five trajectories have five different dash patterns and each prints its own label at the right-hand end, the trained and untrained lines are solid and dashed and both are labelled, the month marker is a dotted rule labelled with its month number, and the five segments of the decomposition bar are named in left-to-right order with their values in the sentence underneath. Each experiment has its own pinned primary and the inactive one is hidden; measured at 1366 by 768 the pins are 355px and 264px, and with the last control of experiment 1 scrolled to the bottom of the window the fan is still at the top of the stage. Nothing animates, so there is no motion to reduce. Every slider, preset and redraw announces through the shell's polite live region, and focus moves to the simulator heading when the prediction unlocks it. Wide tables scroll inside their own containers, heading levels do not skip, forced colours are handled, and there is no horizontal page scroll at 320px, 375px, 1366px, 1440px or 1920px.
tools.readmeTopic: Why four different processes all look like getting better, and what evidence separates recovered function from a better strategy
tools.simulationNotes: An invented model, not data. Severity s runs 1 to 10; capacity just after the injury is C0 = max(5, 100 - 9s) and lost = 100 - C0. Restitution has ceiling lost x (0.55 - 0.035s) and time constant 3 months; relearning has ceiling (lost - restitution ceiling) x rehabilitation intensity x max(0.15, 0.75 - 0.045s) and time constant 9 months; compensation has ceiling min(22, (0.25 x strategy use + 0.12 x environmental support) x lost) and time constant 6 months; practice effects add up to 6 points with time constant 4 months. The trained task is the sum of all five terms capped at 100; the untrained task is starting capacity plus restitution plus relearning, so the gap between the two curves is exactly compensation plus practice. The ceilings shrink as severity rises, so at severity 10 with every slider at maximum the trained task reaches 76 at 24 months and the untrained task 48 - plasticity is not unlimited. In experiment 1 each of five simulated people gets a restitution multiplier from 0.7 to 1.3, a relearning multiplier from 0.6 to 1.4 and a late drift of about N(0, 0.12) points per month after month 6, so some trajectories plateau and some fall; measurement noise is added at every month with SD 2, 5 or 9. Random numbers come from mulberry32 with a visible seed starting at 20260812 and advancing by 7919 on each redraw, with Box-Muller for the normal deviates. Reference values at 9 months, severity 5: Route A (rehabilitation 100 per cent, no compensation) gives trained 86 and untrained 80; Route B (no rehabilitation, strategy use 80 per cent, environmental support 60 per cent) gives trained 86 and untrained 71. Deliberate simplifications: four processes is a caricature and they overlap in time; real trajectories include illness, medication, mood, surgery and life events; rehabilitation is one slider standing for intensity, timing, content, specificity and motivation; no published trajectory, effect size or recovery rate is reproduced; no anatomy is named; and nothing here is a prognosis for anybody.

modules.summary: Tools for social influence and for the critical questions that follow it: who was studied, what a measure licenses you to claim, and where an empirical pattern ends and an interpretation of it begins.

plannedTopics.title: Conformity and social influence
plannedTopics.detail: How group size, unanimity and private versus public response change the pressure a situation exerts.

plannedTopics.title: Attitudes and what a measure captures
plannedTopics.detail: Why self-report, implicit and behavioural measures of the same attitude often disagree, and what follows from that.

plannedTopics.title: Intergroup bias and its measurement
plannedTopics.detail: What group-level findings support at the level of an individual, and the inferential step that is not licensed.

plannedTopics.title: Sampling, generalisability and WEIRD samples
plannedTopics.detail: Which populations the evidence base was built on, and how that constrains the claims that can be made from it.

plannedTopics.title: Constructing the object of study
plannedTopics.detail: How choosing a definition and a measure shapes the finding, and how contested constructs are handled honestly.

tools.title: Epistemology Lens Switch
tools.summary: One fictional school reports a rise in low-level classroom disruption, and the same evidence is given to three research teams with different assumptions about what the social world is. Learners declare a realist/positivist, critical realist or social constructionist starting point and then make five decisions - research object, legitimate question, admissible evidence, method, defensible claim - watching the specification and its coherence change as they go. Running a second lens on the same case produces a side-by-side comparison of what each design makes visible, what it hides and what action it points to.
learningObjectives: State what a realist/positivist, a critical realist and a social constructionist study each take the research object to be.
Explain why the method follows from assumptions about the object rather than the other way round.
Identify the precise claim a given design could support about the same case, and the claim it could not.
Distinguish social construction from fabrication, and coherence from truth.
Recognise when an explanation has been relocated into individuals before any data were collected.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every judgement is evaluated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios, buttons and fieldsets throughout; no dragging and no timing. Only one decision is expanded at a time and collapsing is done by toggling the hidden attribute rather than rebuilding, so keyboard focus survives; focus moves deliberately to the first option of a decision only when a navigation button is pressed. Coherence is always written out in words ('follows from your position', 'in tension') as well as tinted, so no state depends on colour. The study specification is a table, not a diagram, so it needs no chart alternative. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion is honoured; forced-colours rules are provided; the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Same school, same evidence, three epistemologies: how the research object decides the method and the defensible claim
tools.simulationNotes: Meadowbank Academy, its incident counts, staff survey, behaviour policy revision, room moves and focus-group quotations are invented for teaching and estimate nothing. There is no random generation and no seed: the tool is deterministic. Coherence is scored simply as the number of the five decisions whose home position matches the declared position, and the tool states in the interface that this is a minimum standard rather than a measure of quality. Each decision offers a fourth option belonging to a person-centred realism that is not one of the three declared positions; it is included because it is the design a school is most likely to fund, and it is named rather than merely penalised. Three positions is a deliberate simplification of a contested landscape and the tool does not rank them: each lens profile carries what it makes visible and what it costs.

tools.title: Constructing a Category
tools.summary: Nine messy fictional accounts of daily life, and five stages that turn them into a named condition. Learners select the recurring features, choose a name, set a threshold against 400 simulated respondents, build a five-item screening questionnaire and then decide what to do when a training company, an employer, a manager, a newspaper and a funder come calling. The prevalence figure moves from 41% to 0% without one simulated answer changing, and two of the original nine accounts drop out of their own category.
learningObjectives: Identify the specific steps at which a classification acquires the appearance of a naturally given object.
Explain why a prevalence figure is manufactured by a threshold rather than discovered.
Describe what a category name imports before any evidence has been collected.
Recognise criterion contamination, where an instrument restates the criteria it is supposed to test.
State why social construction is not fabrication, and what a critical realist adds to that distinction.
interactionTypes: threshold sliders on a simulated population
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the questionnaire is never administered to the person using the tool, and every calculation runs in the browser tab.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native checkboxes, radios, a range and two selects; no dragging and no timing. The five stages expose only their own controls and their own result, which keeps the controls column short enough for the pinned result to stay in view at 1366x768. Both bar charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables or with counts printed beside every bar, so no band is identified by fill alone; the object-status index is stated in words as well as drawn. Feature counts are printed next to each checkbox so no judgement requires reading the table. Focus moves to the new stage heading when a stage button is pressed. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: From nine accounts to a named condition with a prevalence figure: reification broken into steps you can point at
tools.simulationNotes: The nine accounts, the twelve candidate features, the comparison counts, the five candidate names, the ten questionnaire items and the five institutional events are all authored for teaching; no published category, criteria set, instrument, item or prevalence estimate is reproduced or referred to. Stage 3 uses 400 simulated respondents generated from a seeded mulberry32 generator (seed 20260807) with Box-Muller normal draws: each respondent has a latent load, feature f is present when a uniform draw falls below logistic(intercept_f + slope_f x latent), and duration in months and an interference score are separate draws containing the same latent. A respondent meets the criteria when the number of selected features present reaches the threshold and the duration and interference requirements are met. With the worked-example feature set the prevalence runs 41.3, 37.8, 28.0, 17.3, 7.0 and 0.0 per cent across thresholds one to six, with the population held completely fixed. Stage 4 detects an account when it would endorse three or more of the five chosen items; accounts 7 and 9 are written so that the five most obvious items miss them. The stage 5 object-status index runs from 12 to 100 and is a teaching device, not a measurement.

tools.title: Attitude-Behaviour Gap Laboratory
tools.summary: Four fictional colleagues score 6.2 out of 7 on the same attitude questionnaire about voicing disagreement at work, and then behave on 82, 48, 28 and 14 per cent of occasions. Learners predict each colleague before the model answers, then move six conditions one at a time on a single case, then watch the attitude-behaviour correlation across 300 simulated colleagues change with the setting and with the measure. The key structural point is that opportunity multiplies rather than adds: one colleague has every internal condition the best predictor has, and rarely acts.
learningObjectives: Distinguish a measured evaluation from an action, and say what stands between them.
Explain why some intervening conditions add to the odds while opportunity gates them.
State how measurement correspondence changes an attitude-behaviour association without changing the person.
Explain why the same correlation is larger under uniform conditions than in ordinary teams.
Say what an individual-level model of behaviour represents well and what it makes harder to see.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the questionnaire is never administered to the person using the tool, and every calculation runs in the browser tab.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios, ranges and selects; no dragging and no timing. Each experiment exposes only its own controls and its own result, and the pinned primary result in experiments 2 and 3 is small (125px and 301px) so it stays in view while the controls are scrolled. The contribution chart prints each term's signed value beside its bar and is paired with a visible table, so direction never depends on fill; the scatterplot is paired with a sentence giving the correlation, the group sizes and the two group means. Every slider carries an aria-valuetext in words naming both ends of its range. Focus moves to the new experiment heading when a stage button is pressed. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Four identical attitude scores, four different working lives: what stands between an evaluation and an act
tools.simulationNotes: A small logistic model in the reasoned-action family with every coefficient printed on screen: logit = -1.30 + 2.60 x c x attitude + 1.30 x norm + 1.50 x perceived control + 1.40 x habit - 1.80 x constraint, and p = logistic(logit) x opportunity. All conditions run from 0 to 1; c is the correspondence weight of the measure (0.35 general values, 0.70 behaviour-level, 1.00 matched intention). Opportunity multiplies rather than adds, which is the structural point the tool is built on. The four colleagues are fictional; with the behaviour-level measure they come out at 82, 28, 14 and 48 per cent of occasions. Experiment 3 draws 300 simulated colleagues from a seeded mulberry32 generator (seed 20260419); the same attitude draws are reused in every cell so that no difference between cells can be a sampling difference, and only the variance of the conditions changes. The resulting correlations are 0.69, 0.84 and 0.87 under uniform conditions and 0.20, 0.35 and 0.41 in varying conditions, for the general, behaviour-level and matched measures respectively. None of these numbers is an estimate of anything and none should be quoted as an effect size; a simulation cannot test a theory.

tools.title: Conformity Under Context
tools.summary: A fictional group judgement task with six things the learner can change about the situation, and a model that splits the resulting conformity into a normative route and an informational one.
