Six classic conditions can be loaded and are kept in a comparison table, so the private-response manipulation can be seen to collapse one route while leaving the other untouched. A second experiment opens the headline percentage into the 100 simulated people behind it, a substantial minority of whom never conform at all.
learningObjectives: Distinguish informational from normative influence by the manipulations that move each of them.
Explain why breaking unanimity matters far more than the size of the majority.
Say what group identification adds that the classic two-route account does not contain.
Read a headline conformity percentage as a summary of a distribution rather than a property of people.
Explain why classic laboratory rates are not constants and why the variation between replications is the finding.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; no task is administered to the person using the tool, and every calculation runs in the browser tab.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radios and buttons; no dragging and no timing, and the simulated task is never presented to the learner. Each experiment exposes only its own controls and its own result, and the pinned primary is 125px so it stays in view while the six controls are scrolled. The two-route bar chart prints each route's percentage beside its bar and is followed by a sentence naming both values; the histogram prints each bar's count above it and is paired with a visible table. Every range carries an aria-valuetext in words naming both ends of its scale. Focus moves to the new experiment heading when a stage button is pressed. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Two routes to agreement, six things about the situation, and the distribution hiding inside a conformity percentage
tools.simulationNotes: No historical study is reproduced: not its stimuli, not its procedure, not its data. The presets carry recognisable names so the comparison is legible and their outputs are not those results. Conformity on a critical round is modelled as two independent routes - normative = 0.68 x unanimity x audience x identification x norm clarity, informational = 0.75 x ambiguity x (0.4 + 0.6 x majority standing) x unanimity - combined as 1 - (1 - n)(1 - i). Audience appears only in the normative term, which is what makes the private-response manipulation diagnostic. Unanimity is a step function (1.00, 0.30, 0.22, 0.18 normative; 1.00, 0.60, 0.50, 0.45 informational) rather than a proportion, because a single dissenter matters far more than the headcount. With these parameters the six presets give 35, 12, 14, 66, 7 and 67 per cent. Experiment 2 draws 100 simulated participants from mulberry32 with seed 20260311; susceptibility multipliers are drawn once, normalised to a mean of exactly one so the group average reproduces the headline rate, and rounds are Bernoulli draws from a fixed grid. In the classic condition at twelve rounds, 13 of the 100 never conform at all. The parameters are chosen to put the classic conditions in roughly the right order of magnitude, which is a teaching decision and not a replication.

tools.title: The Self Through Different Lenses
tools.summary: Nine statements by one fictional person, and seven frameworks for the self applied to all of them. Choosing a framework re-weights the shared evidence board into what is central to it, what it can use indirectly and what it has no concept for; the learner then works out which of four genuine accounts of the same person was written from that framework's premises. After four frameworks a synthesis reports what none of them has been able to make central - including a statement about a fee increase and a cut in hours that six of the seven cannot represent at all.
learningObjectives: Apply seven frameworks for the self to the same body of evidence.
State the question each framework asks and the statements it therefore treats as evidence.
Explain why the frameworks are not competing diagnoses of one person.
Identify what a framework backgrounds, as distinct from what its users believe.
Notice what a vocabulary located inside the person systematically cannot record.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the tool asks nothing about the person using it and produces no score for anyone.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios and buttons throughout; no dragging and no timing. The evidence board writes each coding out in words (CENTRAL, usable, no concept) and varies border style as well as tint, so none of the three levels depends on colour; the pinned board is 449px so it stays in view while the seven frameworks and the four candidate accounts are scrolled. Wrong answers produce an explanation of which framework the chosen account actually belongs to and which statements each of the two leans on, never a bare incorrect. Headings do not skip. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Seven frameworks for the self applied to one person, and the statement none of them can use
tools.simulationNotes: Nadia and all nine statements are invented for this activity; no real person, interview or case record is reproduced and nothing here is an assessment of anybody. Each framework carries an authored coding for each statement - central, usable or no concept for it - and these codings are teaching judgements that a specialist in any one tradition could reasonably argue with. There is no random generation and no seed; the four candidate accounts for a framework are selected and rotated deterministically so the correct one is not always in the same position. There is no correct lens and no hidden fact about Nadia: what the tool marks is whether the learner matched an account to the framework that generated it. The codings are arranged to make two structural points - that statement 8, about a fee increase and a cut in hours, is marked 'no concept for it' by six of the seven frameworks and central to none, and that statement 9 is coded differently by frameworks that read it as information about Nadia and frameworks that read it as information about the course.

tools.title: Discourse and Subject Position Laboratory
tools.summary: Eight undisputed events in a fictional woman's six months with a community day service, written up five times: as a case note, a risk register entry, an advocacy bulletin, a recovery-oriented discharge summary and a commissioning report. For each account the learner identifies the subject position it produces, the action it makes legitimate, who it authorises to speak and where responsibility lands, with every wrong option being the right answer for a different account. The ledger of events stays on screen throughout, and one entry in it - the decision that halved the programme's hours - appears in only one of the five accounts.
learningObjectives: Identify the subject position an account makes available to the person it is about.
Say which actions a given position renders reasonable and which unreasonable.
Name who an account authorises to say what is happening.
Trace where responsibility is placed by a description that never mentions responsibility.
Explain why analysing discourse is neither word-counting nor a claim that events are made of language.
interactionTypes: account switching with a pinned text
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the tool asks nothing about the person using it and produces no score for anyone.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios and buttons only; no dragging and no timing. The account being analysed is the pinned primary result at 209px, so its full text stays beside the four questions while they are answered and while the controls column is scrolled. The ledger entry that only one account mentions is marked with a heavier rule and an explanatory phrase in text, so it is never identified by colour alone. Wrong answers explain which account the chosen option is the correct answer for, rather than reporting an error. Headings do not skip. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Same events, five write-ups: subject positions, legitimacy, authority and where responsibility comes to rest
tools.simulationNotes: R, the service, the assessment and all five accounts are invented for teaching; no real person, service, record or document is reproduced and nothing here is a clinical description of anybody. There is no random generation and no seed. Each account carries an authored answer to each of the four analytic dimensions, and the option set for each dimension contains exactly one correct answer per account, so every distractor is the right answer for a different text. The ledger is fixed and every account is consistent with all eight entries: none of the five contains a false statement, which is why accuracy cannot be what separates them. Entry 2, the halving of the programme's hours, appears only in the advocacy bulletin; the other four genres have no field for it, which is the tool's central structural point rather than an accusation of concealment.

tools.title: Norm-Formation Laboratory
tools.summary: Fifteen rounds of a deliberately unanchored judgement: five made alone, five with three simulated others' estimates visible, and five alone again. The three others are generated from anchors drawn around the learner's own opening mean, so the emerging norm is not imposed from outside; the learner's own convergence is never forced or modelled. A final comparison shows three other simulated groups arriving at quite different norms from the identical display, and the historical experiment whose logic the activity borrows is described separately with its criticisms.
learningObjectives: Describe what happens to an unanchored judgement when other people's judgements become visible.
Explain why a frame that persists once the group has gone cannot be explained as compliance.
Account for why different groups reach different norms from the same display.
Distinguish agreeing with an explicit demand from acquiring a shared definition of the situation.
State the boundary conditions on the finding, including the role of ambiguity.
topics: history and criticism of a classic study
interactionTypes: trace chart with full text equivalent
tools.privacy: Estimates are used only to draw the chart in the browser tab and are discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person is produced.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed and nothing is scored; the task is entirely self-paced and a simulated-participant route runs all fifteen rounds for anyone who would rather not answer or is demonstrating from the front. The stimulus is deliberately uninformative and the sentence beneath it carries everything the drawing does, so a learner who cannot see it is at no disadvantage - the ambiguity is stipulated rather than perceptual, and the page says so. The trace chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence listing every estimate by phase with each phase mean; the group phase is marked by a shaded band and by a label inside it. The number input accepts Enter, validates its range and explains a rejected value rather than reporting an error. Changes are announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Alone, together, alone again: how a shared frame of reference forms under ambiguity and outlives the group
tools.simulationNotes: No autokinetic effect is involved and no materials, procedure or data from any historical experiment are reproduced; the display is a drawing with no scale, and the historical study is described separately on the page along with five criticisms. The three other participants are generated only after the learner's first five estimates, from anchors at 0.45, 0.85 and 1.75 times the learner's own opening mean, so the emerging norm is not imposed from outside. On each group round every simulated participant moves 42 per cent of the way towards the running group mean plus noise. The learner's own estimates are never modelled or constrained. The three comparison groups are four simulated participants each, drawn around openings of 0.35, 1.1 and 2.6 times the learner's opening mean and run through the identical rule; in a representative run they arrive at 3.6, 12.4 and 29.3 cm against the learner's group at 11.4 cm. All randomness comes from a mulberry32 generator seeded at 20260214, reseeded on reset. That the demonstration converges is a property of the model; the evidence that people converge is in the literature, not on the page.

tools.title: Minimal Group Allocation Laboratory
tools.summary: The learner is sorted into an arbitrary fictional category on a basis the page immediately admits is meaningless, then allocates symbolic points between one anonymous member of each category, six times. Every option prints its own arithmetic, so the option that gives the learner's own category fewer points in exchange for a larger lead is visible rather than disguised. The same six allocations can then be run in a world where the learner's category already holds four times as much, and in one where it holds a quarter - which makes visible the thing a strategy profile cannot record, that an identical choice creates an inequality in one world and widens an existing one in another.
learningObjectives: Distinguish four allocation strategies and say what each one reveals about the allocator's goal.
Explain why choosing maximum difference over maximum ingroup gain is the finding that no self-interest account reaches.
Describe what social identity theory means by positive distinctiveness and why it is a comparative claim.
State why an allocation pattern between two invented categories is not an explanation of prejudice or of structural inequality.
Judge which conclusions this kind of evidence supports, partly supports and does not support.
interactionTypes: strategy profile chart with full text equivalent
tools.privacy: Allocations are held in the browser tab only, are used solely to draw the profile in front of the learner, and are discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about any person is produced.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed. Every allocation option is a native radio in a labelled fieldset and prints its full arithmetic - points to each side, total, and signed difference - in text, so no choice depends on reading the chart or on colour. The strategy chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence naming all four counts and the running totals; the largest-lead bar is drawn differently but is also named in words. The comparison table is a real table with row headers and a scroll wrapper. The progress checklist marks each item met or not yet in text as well as by marker. Changes, including the category assignment and every recorded allocation, are announced through the shell's polite live region. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Sorted into an invented category, allocating points to strangers - and the option that costs your own side points to buy a bigger lead
tools.simulationNotes: The two categories (Kestrels and Wrens), the sorting question and all six allocation matrices are original and authored for teaching; no published matrix, instruction set or dataset is reproduced. In every matrix the largest-lead option gives the learner's own category fewer points than the own-group-most option does (19 against 25, 15 against 20, 22 against 29, 13 against 18, 18 against 24, 16 against 22), which is what makes the choice between them diagnostic, and the largest-total option always has the highest sum. No simulated respondents are involved and no distribution of choices is modelled: the profile shown is only the learner's own six decisions. The three starting positions - 100 against 100, 400 against 100, 100 against 400 - are this tool's own addition rather than part of the classic paradigm, and are stipulated rather than earned. The worked example runs the pattern fair, largest lead, fair, own group most, largest lead, fair in the equal and already-ahead conditions, producing three fair, no largest-total, one own-group-most and two largest-lead allocations in each, a gap moving from +0 to +25 in the equal condition and from +300 to +325 in the already-ahead condition. Those two rows show the same strategy profile doing two different things, which is the point the comparison table exists to make.

tools.title: Crowd Behaviour Laboratory: Deindividuation and ESIM
tools.summary: One fictional crowd event can be set up five ways - how the police responded, how the crowd read that response, whether a common category was available, what the norm was, and whether people were identifiable. The model reports two things that move independently: how many of six sections of the crowd took part, and how concentrated their action was across four possible targets. A generic deindividuation account predicts the first and is indifferent to the second; the elaborated social identity model predicts the second. Four presets reach the decisive contrasts, including one in which the crowd unites completely and does almost nothing, and one in which the deindividuation description is the better fit.
learningObjectives: State what a generic deindividuation account and the elaborated social identity model each predict about crowd action.
Explain why the two accounts disagree about the patterning of crowd behaviour rather than about its existence.
Describe how indiscriminate treatment can create the shared category it is responding to.
Distinguish anonymity amplifying a salient norm from anonymity removing restraint.
Identify a case in which the deindividuation description fits the evidence better, and say why that keeps the argument live.
tools.privacy: Every setting and judgement is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person using it is produced.
tools.accessibilityNotes: All controls are native radios in labelled fieldsets and labelled selects, and nothing is timed. The target chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence giving all four shares, the even-spread reference and the selectivity value; the police-line bar is drawn differently but every share is printed beside its bar and restated in words. The even-spread reference is a dashed rule and a printed label, never colour alone. The section table marks participation with a Yes or No column, with the heavier rule as a redundant second cue. Every change is announced through the shell's polite live region, including which preset was loaded and what it produced. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, the section-by-section table sits in a scrollable wrapper inside a collapsed details element, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: The same crowd, policed two ways: participation and target selection move independently, and only one account predicts each
tools.simulationNotes: Marlow Bridge and Calder Green are inventions and no real event, policing operation, organisation or person is described; nothing here is evidence for either account, and the model produces the patterns it was built to produce. Nothing is random. Six sections of the crowd carry invented baselines - residents 0.20, campaign regulars 0.40, stallholders 0.12, students 0.28, families 0.04, and a handful who came for a confrontation 0.88. A section takes part when baseline plus unity times legitimacy plus a norm shift reaches 0.60, where unity is 0.10 for differentiated policing, 0.55 for indiscriminate policing without a common category and 1.00 with one; legitimacy is 0.12 when the response is read as reasonable and 0.50 when it is read as unfair; and the norm shift is plus 0.18 for a police-line-only norm, zero for no shared norm and minus 0.45 when confrontation is out of bounds. A section is inside the category once unity reaches 0.55, except the handful who came for a confrontation, who are absorbed only at unity 1.00. Target weights are set by the norm and reshaped by identifiability: where a norm is in play anonymity sharpens it (each weight raised to the power 1.35 and renormalised) rather than broadening it, which is the direction the social identity model of deindividuation effects predicts; where there is no shared norm anonymity moves the weights 40 per cent towards an even spread. Selectivity is the summed absolute deviation of the four shares from 0.25 divided by 1.5, and the disinhibition index is 0.2 or 0.5 for identifiability plus the participation count over 12; both are teaching devices invented for this page and neither is a published measure. The four presets produce, in order: 1 of 6 taking part with selectivity 0.84 and disinhibition 0.28; 6 of 6 with selectivity 0.84 and disinhibition 0.70; 2 of 6 with selectivity 0.08 and disinhibition 0.67; and 1 of 6 with selectivity 0.37 and disinhibition 0.58.

tools.title: Power Lens Laboratory
tools.summary: Nine pieces of evidence about a fictional further-education college and the air in its workshop block. The learner works through the same nine items three times, each time asking a different question of them - who decides and who never has to; what counts as knowing; who is believed and what can be said - selecting the evidence each lens brings into focus and naming what it leaves in shadow. Every pass ends with the remedy that lens implies and a note on what that remedy leaves running. No theorist is named anywhere in the task; the exercise is comparative explanatory analysis on shared evidence, not matching names to definitions.
learningObjectives: Apply three analyses of power to one body of evidence and identify what each brings into focus.
Name, for each framework, a specific feature of the case it leaves in shadow.
State the remedy each analysis implies and what that remedy would leave untouched.
Explain why a framework's blind spot follows from the commitment that makes it useful.
Transfer the analysis to a second case without naming any framework.
interactionTypes: evidence selection against a three-level key
tools.privacy: Every selection is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person using it is produced.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed. The nine-item case file is printed in full, once, as an ordered list above the laboratory, and the evidence picker repeats a one-line version of each item so the controls are usable without scrolling back. All controls are native checkboxes and radios in labelled fieldsets, and applying a lens with nothing selected produces an explanatory message rather than a bare error. The pinned primary is deliberately small - it carries the lens's central question while the learner works down a long list of evidence. Item-by-item feedback names its band in words in every heading, with the coloured left rule as a redundant second cue. The comparison table is a real table with row headers in a scrollable wrapper. Stage progress is carried by the stage track with aria-current and a done state expressed in text. All changes are announced through the shell's polite live region. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: One institutional case, three analyses of power: what each makes visible, what each hides, and what each would have you change
tools.simulationNotes: Brackwell College and Ferrand Borough Council are inventions written for this page; no real institution, incident, inquiry, document or person is described, and no number or quotation is drawn from any real case. Nothing is random and no model is run. Each of the nine evidence items is marked core, partly or no for each of the three lenses, and the overlaps are deliberate: item 4 (the technicians who stopped reporting) is core to the first lens and defensible under both of the others, so a learner who selects it three times is agreed with three times. Core sets are items 2, 4 and 9 for the first lens; items 3, 5 and 6 for the second; items 1, 7 and 8 for the third. The key is one defensible reading of an invented case, written to make the contrasts sharp, and the page says so in the limitations. Theorist names appear only in the teaching notes, never in the task, so that a learner who has never met them can still do the analysis and a learner who has cannot shortcut it.

tools.title: Measuring Prejudice: What Does the Instrument Capture?
tools.summary: Two sequential experiments set in an invented country. In the first, the learner sees one simulated respondent's latency difference score, predicts how many candidates from one region that person shortlisted, and finds out - repeatedly, against a printed base rate, until the difference between a real average association and a useful individual prediction is something they have felt rather than been told. In the second, five instruments (self-report, latency, behavioural choice, informant report and institutional outcomes) are examined one at a time for what each directly observes, what is inferred from it, what alternatives remain and which claim it cannot support. Nothing on the page measures, scores or labels the person using it.
learningObjectives: State, for each of five instruments, what it directly observes before anybody interprets it.
Explain why a small average association supports no prediction about any individual.
Distinguish self-reported attitude, latency measures, observed behaviour and institutional outcomes as four different objects at four levels.
Identify why no individual attitude score can confirm or refute a claim about institutional discrimination.
Recognise the point at which an instrument stops being evidence about a construct and starts being treated as the construct.
interactionTypes: individual-case prediction against a base rate
scatter plot with full text and tabular equivalents
tools.privacy: Every selection is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted. No task on the page measures, scores or labels the person using it - the sorting task is run only on fictional respondents, which is a design decision rather than an oversight.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed and there is no reaction-time task for the learner to perform, so no part of the activity depends on motor speed. The scatter plot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence stating the correlation, the selected respondent's score and what a perfectly predictive score would look like, plus a full table of mean and range by outcome band and a printed rule-accuracy check. The selected respondent is marked by a ring and a full-height dashed stem, so it is found by shape and position rather than colour. Every control is a native radio or button in a labelled fieldset, and requesting a reveal without a prediction produces an explanatory message that treats 'you cannot tell from this score' as a real answer. Both experiments announce every change through the shell's polite live region, and either reset button restores the entire page including the prediction gate. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the first experiment's heading when the gate opens, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: A latency score, a shortlist, a survey and twelve years of appointment figures - four objects at four levels, and none of them is prejudice
tools.simulationNotes: Vantry, the Uplands and the Lowlands are invented and stand for no real population anywhere; the setting was chosen to have no real-world referent so that nothing here can be read as a claim about any actual group. No figure on the page is a prevalence estimate, a norm or a published effect. Experiment 1 generates 200 respondents from mulberry32 seeded at 20260811 with Box-Muller normal draws: a latent association z is drawn, the latency difference score is 0.34 + 0.22z + 0.26e1 seconds, a behavioural latent is -0.30z + e2, the number of same-region candidates shortlisted is round(2 + 0.85 x behavioural latent) clamped to 0-4, and a self-reported warmth gap is 13 + 2.0z + 8e3 points. The construction gives a population correlation of about -0.19, deliberately of the same order as correlations reported in meta-analyses of real latency-behaviour relationships; rounding and clamping attenuate the realised sample value to -0.12. The sample median score is 0.32 s; 43 per cent of the 200 shortlists were even, and a rule that reads a score above the median as 'fewer' is right for 57 per cent of the 114 respondents whose shortlist was not even. The automated twenty-trial run, which always follows the score's direction, typically lands near 25 per cent against that 43 per cent base rate. Every reported figure is computed from the generated sample at run time rather than written into the page. The five instrument findings in experiment 2 are authored for teaching and no published study, dataset or instrument is reproduced or referred to.

tools.title: Person or Setting? Workplace Explanation Laboratory
tools.summary: One fictional team, eleven pieces of evidence and two sequential experiments. In the first, the evidence arrives in three rounds - individual measurements first, then the team and its supervision, then the rota, the queue, the target and a matched comparison team - and the learner commits to an explanation after each round, so the tool can show them their own trail and point out that nothing about the team changed in between. In the second, six costed interventions across three levels compete for a budget that covers half of them, and every modelled outcome ends by naming which pieces of evidence the combination leaves in force, and by reporting that the rank order of the fourteen staff barely moves whatever is spent.
learningObjectives: Construct individual, relational and organisational explanations of the same workplace problem.
Explain why a real, replicable difference between people does not locate its own cause.
State what each intervention targets and precisely what it leaves in place.
Judge the limits of a matched-team comparison that was matched at recruitment and is not matched now.
Resist both the claim that psychological intervention is a distraction and the claim that structural explanation always wins.
interactionTypes: staged evidence release with a recorded answer trail
costed intervention selection against a budget
bar chart with full text equivalent
tools.privacy: Every selection is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person using it is produced.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed. All controls are native radios, checkboxes and buttons in labelled fieldsets, and committing with nothing selected produces an explanatory message that treats 'several at once' as a real answer. Evidence released in later rounds carries a heavier left rule, but each item states its own number and the round heading names what has just arrived, so nothing is carried by the rule alone. Interventions the remaining budget cannot cover are disabled, dimmed, and say so in their own cost line rather than relying on opacity. The outcome chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence giving the before and after scores, the comparison team, the projected leavers and the cost; every value is also printed beside its own bar. Both experiments announce every change through the shell's polite live region, and either reset button restores the entire page including the prediction gate and the other experiment. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the first experiment's heading when the gate opens, the stage track carries aria-current with a done state in text, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: A correlation of 0.61 inside one team, a rota that is the same for all fourteen, and a budget that covers half of what is needed
tools.simulationNotes: Kelbridge Service Centre, its two teams, its review, its exhaustion scale and all its figures were written for this page; no real organisation, team, incident, instrument or person is described, and no number is a norm, a prevalence or a published effect. Nothing is random. Experiment 1 releases four individual-level items, then three relational items, then four items about the work including a comparison team at 38 against Team B's 74; the explanation feedback differs by round and by answer, and round 1 treats the individual-level answer as the best-supported reading of the evidence available, because it is. Experiment 2 starts at a team mean of 74 on a 0-100 scale with three projected leavers of fourteen, and subtracts: resilience workshops 6 (halved to 3 when nothing structural is also chosen, because the conditions reload what the training discharged), coaching for two 1, weekly protected debrief 9, supervisor feedback practice 8, rota and recovery redesign 18, target and discretion change 16, with a further 3 for taking the two relational changes together and a further 5 for taking the two structural changes together. Costs are 2, 2, 3, 3, 5 and 5 against a budget of 10, so the six together (20 units) are unreachable by design. Projected leavers are round(3 x (after / 74) ^ 1.6). The two ten-unit extremes reach 50 (everything individual and relational) and 35 (the two structural changes alone). That the structural combination outperforms is true by construction and is stated as such on the page; the evidence about what works in real workplaces is in the literature, not here.

modules.summary: Tools for trait structure and psychological measurement: where factors come from, what reliability and validity buy you, and why an individual profile is harder to interpret than it looks.

plannedTopics.title: Trait structure and the Big Five
plannedTopics.detail: How correlations among many items resolve into a small number of broad dimensions, and what is lost in the reduction.

plannedTopics.title: Factor analysis, made visible
plannedTopics.detail: Watching a correlation matrix reduce to factors, and seeing how the number retained changes the story.

plannedTopics.title: Reliability
plannedTopics.detail: How internal consistency and test–retest reliability respond to scale length and item quality.

plannedTopics.title: Validity and measurement error
plannedTopics.detail: Why an unreliable measure puts a ceiling on the correlation it can show with anything else.

plannedTopics.title: Reading a trait profile
plannedTopics.detail: Norms, percentiles and the standard error of measurement, and how wide the band around a single score really is.

tools.title: Person–Situation Interaction Theatre
tools.summary: Four fictional characters are put through five situations. Students rank their behaviour twice — once where traits show through and once where a different affordance reorders everyone — then take control of situation strength and assigned role to find the setting where the four become behaviourally indistinguishable.
learningObjectives: Explain what makes a situation strong or weak, and what a strong situation does to observed between-person variation.
Distinguish situational constraint from situational affordance, and explain why two equally weak situations can rank the same people differently.
Explain why low observed behavioural variance is not evidence of low trait variance.
Say why neither 'personality matters more' nor 'situations matter more' is a defensible summary of the evidence.
Relate behavioural consistency to aggregation across situations and occasions.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Ranking uses one native select per character rather than drag-and-drop, so there is no dragging to provide an alternative to; duplicate ranks produce an accessible error message rather than a silent failure. Charts and the interaction diagram are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables carrying the same numbers; edge weights are printed as text beside each edge, and negative weights are dashed as well as signed. Keyboard operable throughout; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Person-situation interaction: situational strength, affordances, and why the debate was badly posed
tools.simulationNotes: Four fictional characters with illustrative trait scores on an arbitrary 0-100 scale; no norms and no reference sample. Behaviour is modelled as k·norm + (1−k)·disposition + role, where k is situation strength and disposition is a weighted sum of only those traits the situation affords. The anonymous-discussion situation carries a negative weight on politeness, which is what reorders the cast. No occasion-to-occasion variability, no measurement error and no trait interactions are modelled. Situation strength is stipulated by the author rather than estimated.

tools.title: State versus Trait Tracker
tools.summary: Simulated experience-sampling data for four fictional people over a fortnight. Students rank them by typical level from a single moment, discover how badly that works, then control within-person variability, measurement error and life events — and watch two people with the same mean turn out to be living quite different fortnights.
learningObjectives: Separate a person's typical level from where they happen to be at one moment.
Explain why within-person variability is a stable characteristic rather than noise to be averaged away.
Explain why measurement error and genuine within-person fluctuation are indistinguishable in one observation and separable across many.
Say how many observations are needed to estimate a person's typical level, and why the answer depends on the person.
Distinguish between-person from within-person variance and interpret the share of variance sitting between people.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Ranking uses native selects rather than drag-and-drop; duplicate ranks produce an accessible error. Four-series line charts distinguish people by colour, by dash pattern and by a name printed at the end of each line, and are hidden from assistive technology in favour of visible tables carrying every summary figure. Sliders announce meaningful values ('measurement error standard deviation 3 points'). The random seed is exposed as a number input so a demonstration is exactly reproducible. Keyboard operable throughout; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: States versus traits: within-person variability, repeated measurement and what a single administration cannot tell you
tools.simulationNotes: Four fictional people on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms. Each observation is trait + decaying event effect + within-person wobble + measurement error, with wobble drawn from a normal distribution whose SD is a property of the person and error modelled separately so the two can be shown to behave differently under averaging. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator; the seed is shown and settable, so any dataset is exactly reproducible. Observations are equally spaced with no missingness, no autocorrelation beyond event decay, and no drift in the trait level — all three are unrealistic and are stated as limitations on the page.

tools.title: Factor Rotation Playground
tools.summary: Twelve fictional adjective markers in a two-dimensional factor space. Students rotate the axes and watch every loading change while the configuration of points, each communality and the total variance explained stay exactly where they were — then meet a genuine cross-loading and a pair of clusters that no orthogonal rotation can fit.
learningObjectives: State precisely what rotation changes and what it leaves invariant.
Explain why rotation neither manufactures results nor identifies a uniquely true solution.
Distinguish orthogonal from oblique solutions and treat the choice as a substantive claim about the constructs.
Recognise a genuine cross-loading as information rather than a nuisance.
Defend simple structure as an adopted criterion rather than a discovery.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, select and buttons; rotation is driven by a slider rather than by dragging, so WCAG 2.5.7 is satisfied by construction. The loading plot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table of every loading, communality and salience decision; markers are labelled by name on the plot itself and the two axes are distinguished by dash pattern as well as colour. Sliders announce meaningful values ('axes 55 degrees apart, oblique solution, factors correlate 0.57'). An invariants box states in words what has not changed after each rotation. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Factor analysis: what rotation changes, what it cannot change, and why simple structure is a criterion rather than a discovery
tools.simulationNotes: Three fictional marker sets with coordinates chosen to make three situations legible: a clean two-cluster structure, one containing a genuine cross-loading, and one whose clusters sit about 55 degrees apart. No correlation matrix was factored and no real study is represented. Rotation is applied as a coordinate transform; oblique solutions read loadings against non-perpendicular axes and report the implied factor correlation as the cosine of the angle between them. Pattern and structure coefficients are not distinguished, the number of factors is fixed at two, and the 'find the simplest structure' control is a coarse sweep rather than varimax, oblimin or promax.

tools.title: Facet-Level Detective
tools.summary: Two fictional people share a broad domain score almost exactly and behave quite differently. Students assign behavioural evidence before the facet scores are shown, build their own matched pair, then watch the "fixed" broad score reverse its ranking when the questionnaire samples facets differently.
learningObjectives: Explain why a broad domain score, being an average of narrower facets, cannot distinguish two people who reach it from opposite directions.
Predict specific behaviour from facet scores rather than from a domain score, and say why the domain score cannot do that job.
State the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off: broad predictors suit broad outcomes, narrow predictors suit narrow ones.
Describe why the facet level is less settled and less reliably measured than the domain level.
Explain how a domain score depends on the questionnaire's item sampling as well as on the person.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native radios, selects, ranges and buttons; each observation is a fieldset whose legend carries the behaviour, so options are never announced orphaned; charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables carrying the same numbers, and every bar prints its own value; verdict tone stated in words as well as by border colour; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Trait structure: what a broad domain score averages away, and the bandwidth-fidelity trade-off
tools.simulationNotes: All people and scores are fictional, on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms, no standard error and no reference sample. A domain score is modelled as the weighted mean of two facet scores; behavioural tendency is a linear function of facet scores with no error, no situational input and no trait interaction. Facet pair names are taken from a published two-aspect account of the Big Five so that students learn vocabulary that exists, but no published item, norm or finding is reproduced.

tools.title: The Alpha Trap
tools.summary: Students maximise Cronbach's alpha by choosing items from a simulated bank, discover that the cheapest route is to ask the same question five ways, and then see the narrow scale they have built fail against a simulated outcome.
learningObjectives: Explain why Cronbach's alpha rises with both the number of items and their average intercorrelation, and why neither is a property of the construct.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of unidimensionality.
Explain why a high alpha is not evidence of validity, using the bloated specific factor as the mechanism.
Judge a scale on content coverage and item redundancy rather than on its reliability coefficient alone.
Recognise that a very high alpha in a short scale is a warning about item redundancy rather than a mark of quality.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout using native checkboxes, radios and buttons; the coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible data table carrying the same numbers; state changes announced through the shell's polite live region; redundancy and outcome verdicts state their tone in words as well as by border colour; stage progress carried by aria-current and visible text; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Reliability: why a high Cronbach's alpha is not validity, unidimensionality or evidence of a good measure
tools.itemSource: All 24 items were written for this tool. No published or commercial questionnaire is reproduced, in whole or in part.
tools.simulationNotes: Every figure is the value implied by a fictional correlation model, not an estimate from a sample. Items load on a general factor, a content-area factor and, for near-duplicates, a wording-specific factor; the simulated outcome responds to the general factor and to breadth of coverage but not to wording. No sampling error is modelled, so no confidence intervals are shown. The construct and its five content areas are invented for teaching.

tools.title: Reverse-Item Disaster
tools.summary: A six-item fictional scale with two reverse-keyed items, scored four ways: correctly, with no recoding, with the wording reversed mentally but not in the data, and with the wrong scale maximum. Totals, item-total correlations, alpha and the respondent ranking all update, and a step-by-step repair mode has students do the arithmetic themselves.
learningObjectives: Recode a reverse-keyed item correctly for a given scale range.
Recognise a negative corrected item-total correlation as the signature of a scoring failure.
Explain why the wrong-maximum error is harder to detect than forgetting to recode entirely.
Distinguish understanding an item as reversed from recoding its numeric response.
State the costs of reverse wording as well as its benefits.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native select, radios, number input and buttons throughout. Every item states its keying in words ('Reverse-keyed') rather than by tint alone, and every recoded answer cell prints the transformation as text ('5 to 1'). The profile chart is hidden from assistive technology and each bar is labelled in text with whether it is the correct or the currently scored total. The repair input accepts Enter as well as the button, and distinguishes the wrong-maximum error and the untouched-number error with specific feedback rather than a generic wrong. Item-total correlations are given a written reading ('negative — flags a problem'). Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Reverse-keyed items: correct recoding, the errors that leave no trace, and why reverse wording is a trade rather than a free fix
tools.simulationNotes: Six original items about persistence written for this tool, answered 1-5 by six fictional respondents whose answers were chosen so the true ordering is unambiguous under correct scoring. No published scale, item or dataset is reproduced. Cronbach's alpha and corrected item-total correlations are computed from the six cases and are illustrative only: statistics from six respondents are wildly unstable and the figures show a direction rather than a magnitude. Four scoring methods are implemented, including two that are arithmetically identical but represent different mistakes.

tools.title: Response-Style Simulator
tools.summary: Seven fictional respondents with the same true standing answer the same twenty items in seven different ways. Students compare raw grids, distributions, totals and split-half correlations, watch balanced keying neutralise acquiescence and unbalanced keying disguise it, then identify a mystery pattern and are asked what it cannot tell them.
learningObjectives: Recognise acquiescent, extreme, midpoint, impression-managed, random, straight-lined and attentive response patterns from their evidence.
Explain why balanced keying neutralises acquiescence and why an unbalanced scale cannot distinguish it from a high score.
Explain why a total score reflects how a person uses a rating scale as well as the trait.
State what a response pattern can establish and what it cannot.
Frame a data-screening decision as a stated methodological choice rather than a judgement about respondents.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Every answer is printed as its own digit inside its cell, so a response grid is readable as text and the shading is a redundant cue rather than the carrier. Reverse-keyed items are marked with a dotted underline and described in the text, never by colour alone. The distribution chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible summary table. Native checkboxes, radios, range and number inputs throughout; sliders announce meaningful values. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Response styles: what a rating pattern shows, why balanced keying matters, and what no pattern can establish about a motive
tools.simulationNotes: Seven fictional respondents sharing one true standing on an unnamed trait, answering twenty generated items on a 1-5 scale. Each style is a transformation of the same underlying response. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator with the seed shown and settable. No real questionnaire, item or dataset is reproduced. Styles are modelled as pure and constant, which real respondents are not; detection uses five simple summary statistics rather than long-string indices, person-fit statistics or response latencies. Impression management is modelled as a shift towards the desirable end and is explicitly not a measure of deception. The tool never attributes a motive to a pattern and marks any answer that does as overreaching.

tools.title: Measurement-Invariance Translator
tools.summary: Two fictional groups, four original items, and full control of loadings, intercepts and latent means. Students manufacture an observed group difference while the true latent difference is exactly zero, see configural, metric and scalar comparisons as pictures before meeting the vocabulary, and find out which comparisons remain defensible.
learningObjectives: Recognise a loading difference and an intercept difference from a graph of item behaviour.
State what configural, metric and scalar invariance each licence you to compare.
Explain why an observed mean difference is not yet a finding about people.
Explain how an item such as speaking up in a group can be harder to endorse at the same level of the trait.
Report which invariance level was reached and confine claims to what it supports.
interactionTypes: multi-select challenge scored against current settings
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, checkboxes, radios and buttons throughout; every slider announces what it controls in words ('how readily this item is endorsed at an average level of the trait'). Each item's parameter group is a fieldset whose floated legend carries the item text, so sliders are never announced orphaned and multi-line legends do not spill out of their box. The item-behaviour panels are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving every loading and intercept and stating in words whether the slope, the level or both differ. The invariance ladder states each level in plain language first, gives its status as the word 'Holds' or 'Does not hold', and names the technical term second. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Measurement invariance: what configural, metric and scalar each licence, and how an item can manufacture a group difference
tools.simulationNotes: Two fictional groups with no nationality, ethnicity, language, region or culture, and four original items written for this tool. Item means are intercept plus loading times latent mean; invariance levels are read directly from the parameters with a tolerance rather than by fitting a model. No fit index, chi-square or p-value is produced, deliberately, because inventing one would teach students to expect a number where real invariance testing gives a judgement built from nested model comparison. Partial invariance is not modelled. Where the tool discusses why an item might behave differently it refers to a setting - whether disagreeing openly is invited or costly - and never to a people.

tools.title: “Explain This Person” Courtroom
tools.summary: One fictional behaviour and eight explanations that all fit it. Students rate each, request evidence, and discover that fitting a case is cheap while predicting something distinctive is not. The verdict rewards evidence that discriminates and proportionate confidence, and scores down anyone who converges on a single cause.
learningObjectives: Explain what underdetermination means for psychological explanation.
Distinguish an explanation that accommodates a behaviour from one that predicts something distinctive.
Identify what evidence would discriminate between two accounts that both fit.
Distinguish competing explanations from compatible ones.
Calibrate confidence to what the available evidence can support.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Each explanation is a fieldset whose floated legend carries the full statement, so rating options are never announced orphaned; the floated legend also prevents multi-line legends spilling out of their box. Native radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout. The competition diagram is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table stating every pair's relationship in words; nodes are labelled and supported/undermined states are conveyed by stroke pattern as well as fill. Requirements tick off in a live checklist with '(met)' / '(not yet)' in the text. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Explanation and underdetermination: why fitting a case is cheap and predicting something distinctive is not
tools.simulationNotes: A fictional case with eight explanations written to be compatible with it, and six pieces of evidence whose findings are stipulated. There is no correct answer and none is stored: the tool has no hidden fact about why the fictional person acted. Explanations are scored on fit and on how much their predictions differ from rivals'; the verdict responds to whether discriminating evidence was requested, whether confidence is proportionate, and whether compatible explanations were kept alive. Distinctiveness is not truth, and the page says so.

tools.title: Intelligence-Test Battery Builder
tools.summary: Seven generic cognitive task families, one testing session, and three different purposes. Students assemble a battery under time and burden constraints, watch breadth, reliability, exposure-dependence and burden trade against each other, then see the same battery judged against all three purposes without a single task changing.
learningObjectives: Explain why validity is a property of a stated use rather than of a test.
Name the constraints that assembling a battery forces into conflict: time, breadth, reliability, exposure-dependence and burden.
Explain why composite reliability rises with test length almost regardless of what is measured, and why that makes it weak evidence of quality.
Explain why removing language from a task reduces some demands without making it independent of prior experience.
Justify a battery against a stated purpose rather than in the abstract.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native checkboxes, select and buttons throughout; each task card carries its costs as text so nothing depends on inspecting a chart. The coverage chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table that states 'not sampled' and 'barely' in words as well as by bar length. Requirements tick off in a live checklist with '(met)' / '(not yet)' written into the text. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Intelligence testing: construct coverage, the trade-offs in battery construction, and validity as a property of a use
tools.simulationNotes: Seven generic task families described in general terms; no published test, subtest, item, norm or scoring rule is reproduced, and no test is named. All values (minutes, reliability, breadth weights, exposure-dependence, burden) are illustrative and were written for this tool. Composite reliability uses Spearman-Brown on the mean task reliability and ignores intercorrelations. 'Fit to purpose' is a weighted sum invented for this tool and is not a recognised index. The tool scores batteries only: it produces no ability score for any person and simulates no group differences of any kind. Exposure-dependence is a property of a task's reliance on prior opportunity to learn its content and is never attached to a person or population.

tools.title: Positive Manifold Visualiser
tools.summary: Six fictional cognitive tasks and a correlation matrix students control by deciding how much of each task's performance is shared with all tasks, shared within a group, or specific and error. Scatterplots, a loading diagram and a genuinely computed first factor follow — and the same positive first factor appears whether the structure underneath is one general ability or two groups.
learningObjectives: State the positive manifold as an empirical pattern rather than as a theory.
Explain why a first factor with positive loadings follows arithmetically from an all-positive correlation matrix.
Recognise that a general factor and broad group factors produce similar first-factor loadings.
Distinguish shared, group, task-specific and error variance and say which of them can contribute to a correlation.
Name rival explanations of the positive manifold and what evidence would be needed to choose between them.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges and buttons; sliders announce meaningful values such as '55% shared by every task'. Every correlation-matrix cell prints its own number so the shading is redundant, and same-group pairs carry a border as well as a tint. The variance bar prints each segment's name and percentage inside it. Scatterplots and the loading chart are hidden from assistive technology and paired with visible tables giving model-implied and observed correlations and every loading, with group membership stated in its own column rather than by bar colour. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: The positive manifold: an empirical pattern, the first factor that follows from it, and why extracting one settles nothing
tools.simulationNotes: Six fictional cognitive tasks in two groups. Each task score is a weighted sum of a general source, a group source, a task-specific source and error, all independent standard normal and scaled to unit variance, so the model-implied correlation is g-squared plus group-squared for same-group pairs. Scatterplots use 220 simulated people from a seeded mulberry32 generator. The first factor is genuinely computed by the power method on the matrix shown, reported as eigenvector times the square root of the eigenvalue, with variance explained as eigenvalue over number of tasks. No real intelligence test, subtest, item, norm or published correlation matrix is reproduced, no ability score is produced for anyone, and the tool contains one undifferentiated population so can support no claim about differences between groups of people. A factor here is described throughout as a property of a correlation matrix and never as a biological entity.

tools.title: Culture-Fair Test Challenge
tools.summary: Students design a non-verbal reasoning task through six decisions and watch six construct-irrelevant demands respond. Removing language removes one of them. Four fictional participants, described only by prior experience of testing formats, show how unevenly a design distributes demands that have nothing to do with reasoning.
learningObjectives: Explain why removing language from a test removes the reading demand and leaves the others intact.
Distinguish construct-relevant from construct-irrelevant demands, and use that framing instead of 'culture-free'.
Explain opportunity to learn a test format as a fact about exposure rather than about capacity.
State what evidence is required before scores from different groups can be treated as comparable.
Recognise that reducing construct-irrelevant demand costs administration time, and is a design decision rather than a discovered property.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native radios, checkboxes and buttons throughout; each design option carries its consequence as text beneath the label. The demand chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table rating each demand 'high', 'moderate' or 'low' in words. The construct-share bar prints its own labels and percentages inside each segment and repeats them in the note beneath, so the split never depends on the fill colours. Participant cards state the load as text as well as showing a meter. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Culture-fair testing: construct-irrelevant demand, opportunity to learn a format, and what comparability requires
tools.simulationNotes: A design model with illustrative values written for this tool; no published test is described. Six construct-irrelevant demands are tracked, combined by maximum rather than sum, and converted to a construct-relevant share by a simple linear rule. The four fictional participants are characterised ONLY by prior experience of testing formats, devices and puzzle conventions: no nationality, ethnicity, region, language or group membership appears anywhere in the tool, and no group difference of any kind is simulated. The tool produces no score, ability estimate or performance prediction for any person, fictional or real; the participant figure is a count of demands the design makes that the person has not had opportunity to become familiar with, and the page states this explicitly wherever it appears.

tools.title: Speed–Accuracy Trade-Off
tools.summary: An untimed arrow-discrimination task students can actually perform, followed by four fictional respondents — three with identical ability and different response caution, one with genuinely lower ability. Speed and accuracy are plotted jointly throughout, and a caution slider moves both at once while ability is held constant.
learningObjectives: Explain why a single outcome measure cannot separate ability from response caution.
Read a joint speed-accuracy plot and locate a respondent on the trade-off curve.
Distinguish a drift-rate (ability) difference from a threshold (strategy) difference.
Explain why reaction-time distributions make the mean and median disagree.
Recognise exclusion cut-offs and correct-trials-only decisions as researcher choices that can move a result.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trials are scored in the browser tab only, nothing is retained after a reset, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: No trial is ever timed out: the stimulus persists until answered, nothing flashes, and the key mapping is stated before any block begins. Untimed practice with feedback runs first. Responses use the Left and Right arrow keys or two large buttons of at least 3.5rem height, so the task is fully operable by keyboard, pointer or touch. The arrow display is aria-hidden and paired with a sentence giving the counts, so a trial is answerable without perceiving nine small glyphs. A complete non-timed route exists: the fictional-strategy simulator and the caution slider reach every conclusion on the page without performing the task, and the page says so before it starts. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a table stating drift rate and threshold outright; the respondent who differs in ability is drawn hollow as well as differently coloured. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Speed-accuracy trade-off: why one outcome measure cannot separate ability from response caution
tools.simulationNotes: Fictional respondents use the standard closed form for an unbiased diffusion process: expected accuracy is the logistic of 2*drift*threshold, and expected decision time is (threshold/drift)*tanh(drift*threshold) plus a non-decision constant. Three respondents share a drift rate and differ only in threshold, so their differing scores are purely strategic; a fourth differs in drift rate instead. No participant, dataset or published parameter estimate is represented. The student's own block is 16 trials, far too few for any real estimate, on browser timing that carries tens of milliseconds of noise. The tool measures nothing about the user: not intelligence, impulsivity, attention or inhibition, and nothing clinical, and the page states this before the task begins and again in the results.

tools.title: Twin-Study Simulator
tools.summary: Students set the true variance components, generate fictional twin and sibling pairs from them, and recover ACE estimates with Falconer's formulae — then switch on unequal environments, assortative mating and gene-environment correlation and watch the estimates fail in opposite directions while the truth stays put.
learningObjectives: State what heritability is a property of: variance in a population under particular environmental conditions.
Explain why heritability says nothing about the causes of any individual's trait, and nothing about malleability.
Derive ACE estimates from MZ and DZ correlations using Falconer's formulae.
Name the assumptions the derivation rests on and say which direction each violation biases the estimate.
Explain why equalising environments raises heritability without any genetic change.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person or their family.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, number input and buttons throughout; every slider announces a meaningful value ('assumption held' rather than '0'). The three scatterplots are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table of pair counts and correlations, and each panel's correlation is also printed as text. The truth-against-estimate table labels every discrepancy 'overestimate', 'underestimate' or 'close' in words. The random seed is exposed so a demonstration is exactly reproducible. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Behaviour genetics: what heritability is a property of, and which way each broken assumption bends the estimate
tools.simulationNotes: Fictional pairs from a seeded mulberry32 generator; 250 pairs per group. Phenotype is a*A + c*C + e*E + m*M with independent standard-normal sources; pair resemblance is produced by the proportion of A and C the pair shares. Estimates use Falconer's formulae. No trait is named and no real study, family or dataset is represented. The model is purely additive: no dominance, epistasis, sex differences, age moderation or gene-environment interaction (gene-environment correlation is modelled). No group comparison of any kind is simulated, and the simulation contains a single undifferentiated population.

tools.title: Gene × Environment Interaction Visualiser
tools.summary: Students name the pattern in a study that sampled only the adverse half of an environmental range, then watch the range widen and the same two groups turn a diathesis-stress finding into differential susceptibility. An explorer then lets them move slopes, crossover and sampled window and see which theory the visible data appear to support.
learningObjectives: Distinguish diathesis-stress, differential susceptibility and vantage sensitivity by the location of the crossover point.
Explain why the range of environments a study sampled can decide which of the three theories it appears to support.
Explain why a significant interaction term does not choose between the three.
State what evidence is needed to claim differential susceptibility rather than vulnerability.
Describe sensitivity as responsiveness in both directions rather than as a defect.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, checkboxes and buttons throughout; sliders announce meaningful values such as 'crossover inside the range'. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving both groups' model-implied outcomes and their difference at three points in the sampled range. The two groups are distinguished by colour, by dash pattern and by a label printed at the end of each line. The pattern the visible data support is stated in words in a live verdict box. Unsampled regions are shaded and described in the readout as a percentage of range sampled. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Gene-environment interaction: how the sampled environmental range decides which theory a study appears to support
tools.simulationNotes: Two fictional sensitivity groups, each a straight line in environmental quality with normally distributed noise, generated from a seeded mulberry32 generator. No gene is named and no genotype appears: the grouping variable is a fictional sensitivity score split for display. No disorder, diagnosis, symptom or clinical risk estimate is used and the outcome axis is an unnamed standardised outcome. No value corresponds to any published finding. Straight lines and a two-group split are deliberate simplifications, both stated on the page; no sampling uncertainty or confidence band is shown.

tools.title: Emotional-Intelligence Claims Laboratory
tools.summary: Six fictional measures - a self-report questionnaire, two tasks with scored answers, colleague ratings of social effectiveness, and the ordinary personality and reasoning measures any claim has to beat. Students read the correlation matrix, test how much of the pattern is method rather than content, run incremental validity properly, and judge five pieces of marketing against the evidence they have in front of them.
learningObjectives: Distinguish convergent evidence from correlation produced by a shared method of collection.
Explain what incremental validity asks that a raw correlation with an outcome does not.
Describe how self-report and maximal-performance measures of the same label can behave differently.
Judge a construct claim against convergent, discriminant and incremental evidence rather than against its plausibility.
Explain construct proliferation and why an attractive label can conceal divergent operational definitions.
interactionTypes: claim evaluation scored against current settings
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every correlation and regression runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it and produces no score for them.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, radios, checkboxes, a select and buttons throughout; every slider announces what it controls in words rather than as a bare number. The correlation matrix is an ordinary table whose cells state their correlation as a number and whose row headers name the collection method, so the tint and the dotted underline marking same-method pairs are reading aids rather than the only cue. The scatterplot is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table giving the pair, the model correlation with a plain-language band, the correlation observed in the simulated sample and the variance shared. Judged claims state agreement in words as well as by border colour. Reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Construct validity: convergent, discriminant and incremental evidence, and what an attractive label can hide
tools.simulationNotes: Six fictional measures described by method type rather than by name. No published emotional-intelligence questionnaire, task, item or scoring key is reproduced, quoted, paraphrased or scored, and no specific test is criticised. Correlations are model-implied: each measure is a weighted sum of independent sources - dispositional, emotion ability, general cognitive, a questionnaire method effect and a testing method effect - so the correlation between two measures is the sum of the products of their shared coefficients. Standardised regression weights are solved from that matrix by Gaussian elimination and the variance accounted for is reported from them. The self-report scale's content is a fixed amount of common variance split between two sources by one angle, so the mix slider redirects the scale without improving it. The numbers are chosen to make a teaching pattern visible and are not estimates of any published finding.

tools.title: Self-Esteem Stability Tracker
tools.summary: Four fictional people share a self-esteem baseline and differ on everything else. Students deliver praise, criticism, success and rejection across three life domains and watch level, day-to-day volatility, domain contingency and recovery speed come apart — four characteristics that a single score collapses into one.
learningObjectives: Separate typical level from day-to-day volatility in self-evaluation.
Explain domain contingency: why the same event moves one person sharply and another not at all.
Distinguish recovery speed from both level and reactivity.
Explain why a single administration cannot distinguish a low level from a position on a recovery trajectory.
Describe variability as an individual difference rather than as a symptom.
tools.privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the tool asks nothing about the person using it, offers no questionnaire and produces no score for anybody.
tools.accessibilityNotes: Native selects, checkboxes, radios and buttons; events are added through selects rather than by clicking on the chart, so there is no pointer-only interaction. The four series are distinguished by colour, by dash pattern and by a name printed at the end of each line, and the chart is hidden from assistive technology in favour of a visible table giving average, day-to-day SD, range and days to return to baseline. Delivered events are listed in text as well as marked on the plot. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
tools.readmeTopic: Self-esteem dynamics: level, volatility, domain contingency and recovery as four separable characteristics
